articles.title: The Diesel Diversion: Trump’s Faulty Attempt to Blame Inflation on Ukraine
articles.body:
The first tanker carrying Russian diesel to the United States since 2022 is expected to arrive in New York within the next few weeks, but its 40,000-ton cargo amounts to less than two hours of American consumption. The shipment will barely register at the pump—and it answers the wrong question, since what drove American diesel past $6 a gallon was never a shortage of Russian supply, but historic bottlenecks from the war in the Middle East.
Recall what happened between May and July of this year, when Ukraine launched one of the most destructive phases of its energy war against Moscow, sending waves of drones attacking massive Russian refineries at Kirishi, Ryazan, Moscow, Nizhny Novgorod, and Omsk one after another. If Russian refining capacity governed American fuel costs, prices at U.S. truck stops should have exploded. Instead, American diesel fell by $1.06 a gallon.
With the midterms days away and September’s consumer price index showing fuel oil up a staggering 74% on the year, President Donald Trump has cast Kyiv as the architect of American inflation. “What’s happened in Russia with Ukraine has been really the biggest problem for diesel,” he said in the Oval Office on September 30 before naming Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy the culprit, telling reporters that Zelenskyy “wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel.”
The charge is politically convenient but economically backward. Until this month’s waiver, Russian fuel had been barred from American ports since 2022, meaning Ukrainian strikes have reached U.S. pumps only through the gradual tightening of global supply. The real shockwave runs through the Strait of Hormuz, where Tehran can choke off a fifth of the world’s seaborne crude overnight. Diesel was $3.48 a gallon in January and still under $4 the week American and Israeli bombs fell on Iran. When Tehran closed the Strait, the price jumped 96 cents in a single week.
From that moment, the U.S. price line has moved in lockstep with the Iran war—cresting at the April ceasefire, dipping only after the June truce, climbing after the pause in hostilities collapsed in July. By September, the tanker war had driven diesel to a record $6.53.
Ukraine’s unceasing drone campaign has at most modestly nudged up the global floor, while the Iran war has steered every spike and plunge.
By authorizing the sale of Russian diesel, Washington provided Moscow the relief that sanctions are meant to withhold. And when Zelenskyy refused to halt strikes on Russian refineries, Americans throttled the Starlink defenses only they can supply.
Now, Ukraine and its European backers are left with a narrowing set of options. Pulled with discipline, however, the levers they hold can still keep Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war on a tightening clock.
A cure that feeds the disease
After an Oct. 9 phone call with Putin, President Trump directed the Treasury to reopen American ports to Russian diesel through April 2027. On paper, the deal promises 4.8 million tons of fuel. In reality, the promise amounts to roughly 10 days of U.S. demand, and analysts doubt that Moscow can ship even that much after months of Ukrainian strikes on the refineries that would fill the tankers.
Carnegie’s Sergey Vakulenko calls the arrangement “largely for show,” yet for a Kremlin watching its September oil and gas tax revenues plunge 22% year-over-year, the spectacle is the prize. What former U.S. Ambassador Michael McFaul condemned as “absolutely deplorable,” and Zelenskyy called “a gift to Putin,” was followed a week later by a concession of far greater strategic weight. Two days before the Russia provisions of the Graham sanctions act were scheduled to bite, an executive order waived them. In a single stroke, the White House neutralized both the 100 and 500% tariffs and stripped out the clause locking existing sanctions in place.
While Moscow collected waivers, Kyiv got the vise. Washington announced an “energy ceasefire” the Kremlin never bothered to acknowledge. After Zelenskyy held his fire for three days, Russia pounded Ukrainian energy infrastructure 76 times in the week that followed. By the Ukrainian president’s account—one Secretary of State Marco Rubio denies—the American satellite alerts that warn Ukraine when a Russian missile is in the air went dark for a period of time. Procurement contracts required for the transfer of an allied-funded batch of Patriot interceptors reportedly sat unsigned on the desk of U.S. Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth.
Meanwhile, the speed of Starshield datalinks, the military-grade Starlink network that Ukraine’s drone units rely on, was throttled. Starshield datalinks need to operate at speeds up to 550 km/h (342 mph) to effectively intercept Russian jet-powered Shahed and Geran drones.
The 160 km/h (100 mph) cap was apparently instituted—simply insufficient to protect Ukrainian civilians from Russian ballistic missiles.
Trump and Elon Musk finger-pointed at each other for the restriction. Trump has reportedly since called Musk to lift the cap. U.S. officials say service is running more normally. Kyiv says the limit remained in place into this weekend, with President Zelenskyy tweeting on October 24 that service has now been restored.
The Trump Administration should also allow Ukraine to use the system in Russia, targeting ballistic missile launchers. Take out the archer, not the arrows.
What Ukraine can still do
Washington’s squeeze rests on the premise that Kyiv is losing and must be forced to settle, but the front-line situation does not support that notion. Russian forces have made virtually no net territorial gains in 2026 despite suffering more than 40,000 casualties a month since July. At this year’s rate of advance, we estimate that Moscow would need 60 years to capture the rest of Donetsk Oblast.
In fact, the momentum has tilted the other way, with Ukrainian counteroffensives, such as the exceptionally innovative Operation Vivaldi. For months, Kyiv’s forces have killed or seriously wounded more Russian soldiers than the Kremlin can recruit. Closing that gap would require a mass mobilization Putin has been afraid to order, wary of unrest in a country reeling from the fuel shortages created by Ukraine’s refinery strikes. The myth of an inevitable Russian victory amounts to a Kremlin sales pitch aimed at Washington, and the very energy campaign the White House wants to shut down is what keeps Putin boxed in.
Nor can the White House physically switch that campaign off. For all the damage the administration’s freeze inflicted on Ukraine’s air shield, enough Ukrainian drones and missiles were able to reach their targets. Washington’s leverage is entirely defensive, whereas Ukraine’s offensive reach is built at home and in Europe. The 1,000-strong armada that struck St. Petersburg in mid-October was built around FP-1 drones, 90% of which are Ukrainian-made, flying into Russian airspace where Starlink does not function, and Starshield caps do not apply. The E.U.’s Kaja Kallas has rightly defended Ukraine’s actions as legitimate self-defense.
By Putin’s estimate, the wider Ukrainian campaign has cost Russia about 1% of GDP, more than a year of Russian growth, as the central bank’s fight against punishing inflation pushed interest rates to their highest level since the early 2000s. The true toll is almost certainly worse. As we have previously argued, even after Moscow blacked out mandatory economic data, the IMF continues to recycle unverified Kremlin figures to dub Russia the world’s fourth-largest economy at peak output, despite ranking just 51st in GDP per capita.
In 2022, hundreds of billions of dollars abandoned the Russian economy after our team helped spur the withdrawal of more than 1,000 major corporations following the invasion. Firms that curtailed operations outperformed those that did not, in terms of market performance.
Even where Kyiv chooses to look beyond oil, its domestic weapons require no American permission and offend no American farmer. Homegrown Long Neptune missiles have already crippled four of the Black Sea Fleet’s Kalibr missile carriers and recently destroyed four Russian Su-34 bombers, proving that Ukraine can systematically hunt the launchers, airfields, and factories that fire on its cities. The same freedom of action applies to striking Russian data centers, an asymmetric campaign that an analyst at the Royal United Services Institute judges lopsidedly in Kyiv’s favor because Ukraine’s critical data is already safely hosted abroad.
Holding an offensive campaign that Washington wants to stop but cannot physically block changes the terms of diplomacy. Toward the White House, Kyiv should act as a customer rather than a supplicant. Any pause in energy strikes should be treated strictly as an opportunity to make a deal—offered only in exchange for verified Russian reciprocity and binding, written guarantees from Washington on Patriot interceptors, satellite-based missile launch warnings, and uncapped Starshield access, a bargain of the kind legislators like Senator Roger Wicker and organizations like the Foundation for Defense of Democracies have urged.
What Europe must now do
Kyiv’s balancing act rests on a hard truth in Brussels. Europe can replace most of America’s financial support and much of its weaponry within two years, but it cannot replace Patriot-class interceptors, space-based ballistic-missile warning, or Starlink-scale connectivity this winter. The vulnerability is partly of Europe’s own making after three decades of over-reliance on American dominance, and it now collides with an American arsenal running dry.
The on-again, off-again war with Iran that drove U.S. diesel to $6.53 is also the conflict that emptied the Pentagon’s magazines. According to an analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), the Gulf conflict consumed roughly two-thirds of America’s Patriot inventory and more than a third of its THAAD interceptors, leaving a rebuild measured in years at the exact moment Ukraine’s Patriot stockpiles are reportedly exhausted. Europe’s scramble to build sovereign air defenses—four SAMP/T NG batteries currently on order, a 10-nation FREYJA program aiming for a first intercept in mid-2027, and the diplomatic courtship of Japan, the sole non-American producer of PAC-3 interceptors—is real and necessary, but slow. Every euro spent on European interceptors is one less dollar earned in Washington, and one fewer armament President Trump can delay.
A similar bottleneck applies to space. While Europe’s radar and optical satellites could potentially replace American targeting imagery within weeks, OneWeb and the E.U.’s GovSatcom offer only a partial hedge against a Starlink slowdown. And a European satellite constellation capable of warning of a ballistic launch probably will not exist before the 2030s.
Because Europe cannot buy its way out of those technical bottlenecks overnight, it must lean aggressively into the financial and maritime levers it controls today. The E.U.’s €90 billion loan covers 2026 and much of 2027, and when the remaining €70 billion gap comes to a head at the December European Council, moving the €202 billion in frozen Russian assets out of Belgium offers the clearest route around Belgium’s objections. Better still, a full ban on shipping services for Russian crude, along with expanding the shadow-fleet boardings that European navies have already begun, could squeeze Moscow’s war chest at almost no cost to European taxpayers.
Ukraine’s most decisive advantage, though, is found on the factory floor. Domestic drone production has surged 370% this year, and the Ukrainian-made Flamingo cruise missile costs just under $600,000, less than a fifth of an American Tomahawk’s $3.5 million price tag. By guaranteeing a loan to the Flamingo’s manufacturer, Denmark has laid out a blueprint for surviving an erratic Washington: European capital behind Ukrainian weapons.
The lesson of the lever
A bitter paradox governs the current battlefield. The offensive campaign squeezing Moscow is the one Washington objects to, while the defenses faltering over Ukrainian cities are the ones only the U.S. can supply. By blaming Kyiv for an energy shock originating in the Persian Gulf, the White House has struck a bargain that lowers no prices at home, replenishes the aggressor’s coffers abroad, and teaches the Kremlin that American sanctions expire if Putin simply waits them out. Such a posture delivers neither peace nor strength.
Ukraine is akin to the Biblical hero David, who, through cunning, triumphed over the lumbering giant Goliath. Moscow's “card hand” is neither the colossus Trump believes it to be nor the colossus its propaganda advertises. Russia is not remotely an economic superpower. Beneath its vast map lies a concentrated population—over 80% of the population lives in the 20% not plagued by extreme cold, permafrost, and poor soil—and a brittle economy dependent on raw materials the world can increasingly buy elsewhere, backed by a military with a long history of failing to subdue smaller, more determined foes, from Japan in 1905 and Poland in 1920 to Finland in 1940 and the Afghan mujahideen in the 1980s. Sheer land mass has never guaranteed victory when the smaller side is fighting for its existence.
The silver lining is that Washington’s attempted coercion is forging the European autonomy it assumed would never materialize. If European leaders withstand Russian pressure over the next 18 months and resist the political disarray stoked by Kremlin disinformation, the continent will emerge a far more formidable power—proving the quip circulating in allied capitals that Europe has found no better unifier since Charlemagne than Donald Trump. Europe, Ukraine, and the world now know what an American guarantee is worth when the guarantor changes its mind, and Washington is about to learn that leverage, like interceptors, is a stock that depletes with every use.
As Mark Twain advised, “It’s not the size of the dog in the fight; it’s the size of the fight in the dog.”

articles.title: France Brings 10 European Allies Into Its Nuclear Deterrence Plan Against Russia
articles.body:
- Category
- World
France Brings 10 European Allies Into Its Nuclear Deterrence Plan Against Russia
France is expanding its nuclear deterrence posture across Europe in response to nuclear threats from Russia, increasing its warhead stockpile for the first time in decades and placing its arsenal size under total secrecy, as reported by The Wall Street Journal.
As the only European Union member state possessing nuclear weapons, France holds approximately 290 nuclear warheads and is scaling up production while ending public reporting on its stockpile.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The move extends nuclear deterrence in Europe beyond the US nuclear weapons stored in five European countries under NATO’s nuclear sharing program. France has reached agreements with 10 European countries to join the strategic initiative: the United Kingdom, Germany, Poland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Greece, Finland, Norway, Sweden, and Denmark.
The framework centers on temporarily deploying nuclear-capable French Rafale fighter jets across Europe alongside the construction of specialized infrastructure, new communication systems, early warning capabilities, and intelligence-sharing mechanisms.
French President Emmanuel Macron has described the expanding nuclear umbrella as “advanced deterrence,” intended to complicate strategic calculations for Russia, The Wall Street Journal reported.
Xavier Chatel, strategic advisor to the French president, stated that the initiative provides France with “new options for positioning nuclear forces in the event of nuclear escalation.”
Military experts note that this setup poses a more immediate tactical challenge for Russia than NATO’s traditional nuclear sharing program. Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide noted that France holds a strategic capability that complements existing US security guarantees.
Analysts highlight that French ASMP-A cruise missiles carried by Rafale jets are designed to target major Russian cities with a high probability of reaching their targets, establishing a distinct level of deterrence.
Nicole Grajewski, a Russian and nuclear policy expert at Sciences Po in Paris, observed that while it remains unclear whether the posture will convince Russian strategists that France would risk a retaliatory strike on Paris for allies like Warsaw, Russian military officials are actively monitoring the expansion, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Earlier, Germany and France put their nuclear-deterrence cooperation into practice for the first time, staging a joint air force drill with nuclear-capable French Rafale jets and German Eurofighters.

articles.title: Ukraine Asks 5 European Allies for Patriot Missiles
articles.body:
Ukraine has asked five European partners to provide 10% of their existing stocks of interceptor missiles for Patriot and IRIS-T air defense systems to help protect the country against Russian attacks, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said.
The request was directed to the UK, France, Germany, Italy, and Poland. Khmara said Ukraine had already signed contracts for future deliveries of interceptor missiles and proposed an exchange that would allow Kyiv to receive ammunition immediately.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Ukraine already has contracts in place for future deliveries of interceptor missiles, so it is proposing an exchange: partners would provide a portion of their current stocks now, in return for the shipments that are scheduled to arrive in Ukraine later,” he said on Telegram.
Ukraine’s Armed Forces (AFU) also urgently need additional man-portable air defense systems (MANPADS), he added.
“Ukraine is counting on funding for new acquisitions, as well as the transfer of systems from the existing stockpiles of its partners,” Khmara said.
The minister added Ukraine could double its drone production by 2027 if funding arrived on time. Kyiv is proposing not only to increase procurement but also to expand joint production of Ukrainian drones abroad.
“We are proposing not only to increase procurement but also to scale up the joint production of Ukrainian drones in other countries,” Khmara said. He added that the approach would help Ukraine obtain the drones it needs while strengthening the defensive capabilities of partner countries.
Ukraine Confirms Honoring US-Brokered Truce in Russian-Occupied Oleshky
European allies prepare winter aid
Following a meeting in Paris with defense ministers from the UK, France, Italy and Poland, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said the participating countries had already prepared winter aid packages for Ukraine.
“Moreover, we will do everything in our power to ensure that the United States continues to support Ukraine – through its own shipments, and, above all, by providing intelligence and satellite data,” Pistorius said.
He added that European countries were working with Kyiv to develop an air defense system.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia was preparing to intensify attacks on major Ukrainian cities.
Senior Ukrainian officials told The Economist that Moscow planned to paralyze Kyiv before the onset of colder weather in an effort to destabilize the political situation. According to the officials, Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered attacks on civilian infrastructure across the capital.
Separately, Ukrainian officials told the Financial Times (FT) that Moscow intended to increase pressure on Kyiv in hopes of forcing Ukraine to accept Russian demands, including surrendering territory in the Donbas, by early 2027.
Ukraine has waited nearly a month for Patriot missiles
Ukraine will again raise the issue of delayed air defense missile deliveries with the US, as Kyiv has been waiting nearly a month for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to approve missiles for Patriot and NASAMS systems, Zelensky said on Monday.
Zelensky added that he had instructed his team to raise the issue with Washington again. Ukraine is also seeking PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors from EU countries and other partners holding existing stocks.
The shortage comes as Ukraine struggles to secure enough ammunition to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks. Zelensky previously said Ukraine had received just 24 Patriot interceptors from the US over 90 days, despite requiring around 350 per month.
He has also asked European partners to provide 300 interceptors for the winter, but efforts to obtain missiles from existing stockpiles have faced resistance, including from Greece.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian Air Force official Yuriy Ihnat said that missiles expended in the Middle East could have sustained Ukraine’s Patriot systems for several years.
He said Ukrainian crews had developed more efficient tactics, typically using one interceptor per target and employing ambushes before quickly relocating systems. By contrast, air defense forces in the Middle East have reportedly fired as many as eight interceptors at a single target, including relatively cheap Shahed drones.
Zelensky also called for faster implementation of decisions expected to support Ukraine’s air defense, as officials prepare for the next Ramstein-format meeting in November. “Every support package is an opportunity to protect people’s lives,” he said.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Satellite Disruption Exposes a Central Risk of Modern Warfare
articles.body:
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk claimed over the weekend that the Ukrainian military had “violated” the terms of service for Starlink, the company’s commercial satellite internet network, which has become central to the country’s defense against Russia. Musk said SpaceX had restricted Starlink to prevent that alleged misuse. Ukrainian officials disputed his claim. His allegation came after over a week of uncertainty about why the services had been restricted.
Ukrainian officials reported on Oct. 14 that restrictions affecting SpaceX’s satellite communications were disrupting drone operations, blocking a key line of defense amid daily Russian air attacks. Ukraine relies heavily on Starlink for frontline communications, drone capabilities, and reconnaissance; the throttled connection ultimately led to the cancellation of several missions, officials said.
The restrictions also affected Starshield, a military-grade satellite communications service that uses Starlink technology but is supplied through U.S. government contracts.
Over a week after the disruption began, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said on Oct. 24 that both services had been fully restored. It reported that connections remained stable even when terminals were moving at speeds above 400 km/h.
At the time, the cause for the interruption had not yet been clarified, but Defense Minister Yevheniy Khmara emphasized the importance of a strong and stable connection, calling it “vital for our front line, for our military personnel, for the operation of drones, and for logistics and communications.”
Musk maintains that the United States government controls changes to Starshield, leaving questions about who authorized its restrictions—and why.
U.S. President Donald Trump declined to identify those involved in the decision, while a Reuters report from Oct. 15 cited multiple officials who said the order came from inside the White House. The sources did not identify who authorized or implemented the restrictions, but a senior U.S. official denied that it was Trump, the report said.
Experts say that the disruptions expose a growing vulnerability in modern warfare: military reliance on a single private technology supplier.
The company that controls the technology can ultimately wield significant influence over military operations, leaving governments dependent on decisions made by executives and billionaire owners outside traditional diplomatic channels, experts warn.
Why U.S. control of Starshield matters for Ukraine
Ukraine’s access to satellite communications depends on decisions made in Washington as well as at SpaceX. That leaves Kyiv navigating both a private supplier’s restrictions and a fraught relationship with the Trump Administration.
In recent weeks, Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for rising global fuel prices and called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to stop those attacks—despite the fact that experts have primarily attributed the price surge to the U.S. war with Iran.
Trump said on Oct. 15 that Zelensky was “more difficult to deal with” than Russian President Vladimir Putin and on Oct. 19 suggested that it was “time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine.”
Alex Crowther, an adjunct professor at Florida International University’s Jack D. Gordon Institute for Public Policy, says the Starshield dispute goes beyond Trump’s souring relationship with Zelensky to a more basic question: Who has the authority to restrict Ukraine’s access?
“Usually when [a foreign entity] signs a contract with an American company, it says who has the capability to turn this stuff on and off, and the circumstances under which they can turn it on and off,” Crowther says, questioning who has that authority over the services Ukraine relies upon. “Is it Starlink, which is private, or is it Starshield, which is an American government contract? Is it Musk? Is it Hegseth? Is it Trump?”
“Nobody knows the rules right now,” he says.
Lance Hunter, a professor of political science at Augusta University, tells TIME that this dispute exposes the potential issues of having three different actors—the Trump Administration, SpaceX, and Ukraine—with potentially incompatible priorities.
How dependence on SpaceX limits Ukraine’s military autonomy
Hunter says that what is unfolding in Ukraine underscores warfare’s growing dependence on digital technology. Beyond traditional “tanks, bombs, planes,” he says that includes factors like artificial intelligence, drones, and navigation jamming.
Reliance on ongoing technology services creates a different relationship from a traditional arms purchase, Hunter says.
He points to traditional arms deals in which a private company sells a government a set amount of missiles or interceptors.
“Let's say you purchase a piece of weaponry or vehicle or any type of object that helps you in the conflict: You own it at that point. You have control over it,” Hunter tells TIME.
The relationship between Ukraine and SpaceX, however, is different; purchasing the technology does not guarantee operational sovereignty.
“Ukraine has a lot of transmitters which interface with Starshield and Starlink, and they're very much dependent on SpaceX as far as allowing them to use those when they need to,” Hunter continues. “There's not just a one-time dependence buying the technology; it's continual now.”
That gives the company more “influence and leverage” over conflicts than it has before, he adds.
It shifts the way that countries like Ukraine need to think about who they are willing to work with and how they weigh the potential costs.
Why Ukraine cannot easily replace Starlink and Starshield
In a perfect world, Hunter says, Ukraine would diversify its technology suppliers to decrease reliance on Starlink.
The country has already been expanding its domestic weapons production, including interceptor drones. But it remains dependent on foreign suppliers for critical air-defense weapons like the U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles.
That dependence has left it vulnerable to shortages and delays. On Oct. 26, Zelensky said Ukraine had been waiting nearly a month for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to approve supplies of missiles for its Patriot and NASAMS air-defense systems.
But replicating satellite communications networks presents a different challenge. Starlink technology is not something a government can easily reproduce domestically, Hunter says, and few providers worldwide offer comparable capabilities.
“Starlink has a monopoly on that technology to a degree, as far as the speed, the availability, the flexibility,” he says. “It's not like they can just flip a switch and diversify that technology. It takes a lot of time. It takes a lot of resources. It takes a lot of effort, and also in Europe we don't see that same level of technology with some of the European countries and also with some of the private companies.”
In the end, he says that Ukraine is stuck between “a rock and a hard place” as the country tries to negotiate its relationships with the Trump Administration and, separately, with Musk.
“You're reliant on the politics of those bodies all matching up,” he says of Ukraine. “All of a sudden, you kind of lose that autonomy.”
“If they really push back against the U.S. government or SpaceX, they have the potential of receiving less of the technology and being cut off to a greater extent,” he adds. “But if they don't really push at all and advocate for their interest as well, then they could be in a weaker position as far as having leverage exerted over them.”
Why Ukraine disputes Musk’s Starlink claims
In a social media post on Oct. 24, Musk said that SpaceX had restricted Starlink access deliberately because Ukraine's military violated Starlink's terms of service by using the civilian satellite network for offensive drone strikes.
“Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” Musk said in one post. “Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be.”
Musk explained that Starlink continues to be “critical to the defense of Ukraine,” but that it could not be used for offensive military operations.
Ukrainian officials promptly disputed Musk’s claims.
Defense technology adviser Serhii Beskrestnov wrote in a Telegram post that operational and speed restrictions are in place that make it “physically impossible” for the military to use Starlink for medium- or deep-range offensive strikes.
“It is very strange that Elon Musk is unaware of the operational limitations of Starlink in Ukraine,” he wrote. “Starlink does not function over the territory of Russia.”

articles.title: Upgraded Russian cruise missile crashes in Ukraine
articles.body:
- Photos show Russia’s upgraded Geran-5 K5-K light cruise missile, serial number ANS-3031, lying in a field in Ukraine’s Odesa region.
- The new version has a redesigned airframe and modern navigation equipment, and the cause of its crash is not yet known.
Photos have emerged of Russia’s newest version of the Geran-5 light cruise missile, known as the Geran-5 K5-K and often described in the media as a jet-powered drone, lying in a field somewhere in Ukraine’s Odesa region after it came down during an attack, with the serial number ANS-3031 visible on the airframe.
It is not yet known why the Geran-5 K5-K crashed, whether it was hit by Ukrainian air defenses, brought down by electronic warfare or failed on its own, and Ukrainian officials have not commented publicly on the find.
The K5-K is an upgraded version of the Geran-5 cruise missile with a noticeably different design from the first versions of the weapon, and Ukrainian sources say the new variant has a modified fuselage, smaller swept-back wings, a tail without wingtips and an engine moved from an external pod into the fuselage, along with more modern navigation equipment.
Russian forces began using the new version in late September, and Ukrainian defense technology adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov has said it carries autonomous optical navigation that compares images of the ground below with stored data to correct its course without satellite signals, which makes it much harder to throw off course with jamming, while its designers are reportedly aiming for speeds of up to 900 km/h (559 mph).
Russia first used the original Geran-5 against Ukraine in early January 2026, when Ukraine’s military intelligence described it as a turbojet-powered weapon with a conventional cruise-missile layout, a warhead of about 90 kg (198 pounds) and an advertised range of roughly 1,000 km (621 miles), and said its design was substantially similar to Iran’s Karrar.
Ukrainian intelligence data give the baseline Geran-5 a length of about 6.5 meters (21 feet), a wingspan of 3.2 meters (10.5 feet), a takeoff weight of up to 850 kg (1,874 pounds) and a cruising speed of 450 to 600 km/h (280 to 373 mph), using a Chinese-made Telefly turbojet, a Kometa anti-jamming satellite navigation receiver and cellular modems.
Ukraine’s Defence Intelligence has said Russia produces about 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 weapons a month at the Alabuga plant in Tatarstan, and that Moscow has been building additional production facilities there since May 2026.

articles.title: New report tracks how Russia helps China build better drones
articles.body:
Russia's defense cooperation with China extends far beyond imports of dual-use goods, with evidence pointing to sharing drone design technology, providing testing services, and joint research, according to a new report from U.S. think tank C4ADS.
The report adds to earlier findings by the Kyiv Independent regarding China's military collaboration with Russia throughout the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
C4ADS, a Washington-based nonprofit that investigates security threats, released a report in October that maps lesser-known layers of cooperation between the two countries' defense industries, drawing on Russian trade records, corporate filings, leaked documents, and academic papers.
The investigation found that Russian designs for rocket-launched drones likely helped shape weapons China unveiled in 2025 and that Russian wind tunnels kept testing aircraft models for China's top arms maker after the invasion of Ukraine.
The report also documents how researchers from the two countries are jointly developing algorithms that could underpin combat drone swarms. Moreover, it shows that some suppliers to Russia's defense industry are moving production to China.
Beyond China’s well-documented supplies of components, raw materials and machine tools to the Russian defense industry, and Russia's recently revealed sales of airborne combat vehicles and munitions to China, the two industries increasingly work together further upstream, sharing designs, testing services and research.
read also
Joint drone development
A notable example involves the Science and Production Association SPLAV, Russia's leading maker of multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS). SPLAV is subject to multiple international sanctions and export controls.
Trade records show SPLAV sent Chinese arms giant Norinco technical documents for a "reconnaissance rocket" in 2014–2015, and apparently again in April 2022, less than two months after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The rocket is most likely SPLAV's 9M534, which releases a reconnaissance drone in mid-flight.
In March 2025, China unveiled the Feilong 60A, a loitering drone launched from Norinco's SR-5 rocket system and reportedly capable of operating in swarms. Three months later, Norinco tested Sky Eye, a drone fired from a cannon. Both drones are similar to the Russian 9M534.
C4ADS believes the Russian technical documents helped speed up Norinco's work on both systems, though it notes that this conclusion rests mainly on how closely the Chinese and Russian systems resemble each other.
Russia's aerospace testing base is also working for Norinco, which now faces U.S. sanctions and Japanese and Taiwanese export controls.
The Russian state-owned Central Aerohydrodynamic Institute (TsAGI), which is under multiple Western sanctions, tested Chinese scale aircraft models in its wind tunnels and returned them to Norinco with the test data at least nine times between 2022 and 2024. The work comes as Norinco has been expanding into military drones over the past decade.
read also
The cooperation also extends to universities and research institutes. Drones have become a growing focus of joint research by Chinese and Russian scientists, according to C4ADS.
Researchers from the two countries co-authored 86 academic papers on drones and other unmanned systems between 2022 and 2026, an average of about 17 a year. In the dozen years from 2009 to 2021, they produced only 36 such papers, or about three a year.
Evgeny Neretin, a department head at the Moscow Aviation Institute, has co-authored multiple papers with researchers tied to Chinese defense laboratories — labs that also funded the work. The papers deal with algorithms for autonomous drone combat and, more recently, for keeping several drones in formation while they track targets, a likely building block for drone swarms.
In June 2025, the Chinese government approved the creation of a joint educational institute between the Moscow Aviation Institute (sanctioned by the U.S. and EU), and China's military-linked Northwestern Polytechnical University (subject to U.S. and Japanese export controls).
read also
Russian weapons, made in China
The C4ADS report also indicates that some Russian makers of machine tools and chips are moving production to China.
Stankomashstroy, a sanctioned Russian machine-tool maker, plans to move production of advanced five-axis machine tools to an industrial park in China's Shaanxi province.
In 2025, the company sold equipment to the Votkinsk Plant, which builds ballistic missiles, and to Izhevsk Electromechanical Plant Kupol, a producer of air defense systems and long-range attack drones.
Illustrating Moscow's reliance on Beijing for chips, Russia's sanctioned state-owned chipmaker Element set up at least four subsidiaries in China in 2025 and began assembling chipsets there. In 2026, Element also bought power electronics intellectual property from the Chinese defense contractor Shijiazhuang Tonhe Electronics.
According to C4ADS, these moves would likely help Element produce military-grade microelectronics despite Western sanctions and export controls. They also fit a recent Kremlin initiative to build up Russia's chip industry.
A deepening alliance
The C4ADS report adds fresh details to previous findings by the Kyiv Independent regarding China and Russia's military partnership.
While China officially claims neutrality in Russia's war against Ukraine, Beijing remains Moscow's key trading partner, economic supporter, oil buyer, and provider of dual-use equipment.
According to leaked Rostec documents, China bought Russian airborne combat vehicles, ammunition, and parachute systems after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Dozens of Chinese officers and arms industry staff visited Russia during the war to negotiate the deals.
Separate Kyiv Independent investigations found that Chinese suppliers have helped keep Russia's missile and drone production pipelines running.
Machine tools shipped mostly from China fueled the expansion of the Votkinsk Plant, which makes ballistic missiles — including intercontinental ones.
Chinese and Hong Kong companies also supplied parts to the maker of Russia's Lancet attack drones and remain the main channel for Western chips used in Russian weapons.

articles.title: Russia launches 280 drones at Ukraine as local ceasefire begins in Oleshky – Europe live
articles.body:
Norway's Støre defends Putin call, but acknowledges 'significant' differences in opinions
Jakub Krupa
Norway’s Jonas Gahr Støre has offered a bit more colour on his and Stubb’s call with Russia’s Putin in a huddle with journalists in Helsinki just now.
He and Stubb had been initially given only 20 minutes to talk to Putin, but ended up speaking for 90 minutes, in a conversation he described as “substantive, focused on the issues at hand, and professional.”
“Much of what he said was already known – he [Putin] recalled his views on how the conflict evolved since 2014 – and we stated our positions. These are well-known views, which we were able to acknowledge and respond to,” he said.
The talks touched on what can be done to tackle most pressing issues, including attacks on energy infrastructure and in the Black Sea.
But Støre conceded “there remain significant differences in our respective positions,” reiterating Norway’s continued support for Ukraine.
“We stand with Ukraine, defend its right to self-defence, and emphasise the need for a diplomatic path to end this war in a lasting and just manner,” he said.
Støre also stressed that he and Finland’s Stubb spoke on behalf of their two countries only, “and no one else.”
Responding to criticism of their call from Denmark’s Frederiksen(11:26), he said that “all our partners and allies were informed in advance and received a detailed account afterwards.”
Pushing back further, he added:
“If one assumes that the current situation – where communication from the American administration to Moscow serves as the sole channel for discussing Ukraine outside of Ukraine – is the only way, then one is entitled to that view. I believe it is important that other voices are heard as well.”
Støre also stressed that the importance of the meeting in Abu Dhabi, first agreed as a result of the Oslo consultations that he and Stubb hosted.
In a brief section of the briefing in English, Støre again focused on pushing back against Frederiksen’s criticism:
“I believe that talking, having the right messages, is not wrong. Today these messages [are] coming out of the American administration; that is the only thing reaching Moscow. So [now] there are [also] voices from two neighbouring states, speaking on behalf of Finland and Norway, not speaking on behalf of others, but … in full compliance with the coalition of the willing who share view on the nature of this war and how with has to end.”
No solution to end the war can be found without Ukraine's involvement, Merz says
German chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Tuesday that attempts by the US and Russia to end the war in Ukraine “can never find solutions without Ukraine” and said any talks must also include European countries.
Merz was speaking at the Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore as he described diplomatic efforts to build a negotiating format with Moscow.
He said the end of the war depended “only on one person” and framed continued backing for Kyiv as a defence of Europe’s political order.
He said “as long as he [Putin] does not want to end the war, we will support Ukraine” and that Europe was not just defending Ukraine’s territorial integrity but also “the entire political order of the European continent”.
Merz added that Russia, Ukraine, the United States and European countries should be at the negotiating table and warned against a scenario where “Russia, perhaps China and the United States of America” end the war without Ukraine.
Stubb talked of 'very restrained optimism' about constructive peace talks in Abu Dhabi, Tusk says
Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk has also responded to Stubb and Støre’s engagement with Putin, giving a detailed account on the European consultations ahead of and after the call.
Speaking before the cabinet meeting in Warsaw, Tusk said the call followed “consultations with me, among others, but primarily with president Zelenskyy and the US side … that it would be good for European politicians to have a working contact given the planned ceasefire talks that may take place in Abu Dhabi.”
He said the UAE talks between Russia, Ukraine, and the US are provisionally planned for 4 November.
Tusk confirmed he had been briefed on plans for the call beforehand, with Norway’s Støre assuring him that he and Stubb were ready to take political responsibility for this rare engagement with Putin, and would stick to the agreed position of the coalition of the willing.
He said Finland’s Stubb then briefed him after the call, saying “both sides maintained their positions,” and that “the European side’s impression during the call was one of very restrained optimism” about the chances of making progress in Abu Dhabi.
Tusk said he was “very cautions” about engaging with Russia and urged Stubb and Store to be “vigilant” in their talks with Putin, as “Russia’s agenda and interests are quite precisely defined, and that one should harbour any illusions about getting an agreement.”
He said Stubb and Støre also told Putin that the security of Nato’s northern and eastern flanks were “non-negotiable”.
Poland’s PM also stressed that despite the resumed dialogue, “nothing changes” in Europe’s “full support for Ukraine,” or collective views on “the [broader] security architecture and security guarantees for Ukraine.”
Summing up the talks, he said:
“We should not have any illussions; it is clear what the Russian side is playing at, but I will remain in constant contact with all those who possess the good will and the belief that an agreement is possible – or at the very least, a ceasefire before winter.”
Without specifying the source of his claim, Tusk said that “three, four nights ago,” “Russia lost 2,500 men” during one night. “This gives us an idea of just how dire the further consequences of this war could be.”

So [now] there are [also] voices from two neighbouring states, speaking on behalf of Finland and Norway, not speaking on behalf of others, but … in full compliance with the coalition of the willing who share view on the nature of this war and how with has to end.”
Russia is exploring the possibility of cooperation with partners from the United States in the resource-rich Arctic, president Vladimir Putin told a conference of gas-exporting countries in Moscow.
Putin did not specify whether the joint projects under consideration would involve extracting natural gas or other resources.
Russia says three tankers with diesel en route to US
Three tankers carrying Russian diesel are en route to the United States, with a fourth expected to depart Wednesday, Moscow said, part of a deal that triggered a fierce Ukrainian and European backlash.
US president Donald Trump this month struck an agreement with Russia’s president Vladimir Putin to ease sanctions in exchange for Moscow releasing diesel onto global markets.
The measure was seen as an attempt to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of the US midterm legislative elections on 3 November and drew sharp criticism from Ukraine and its allies.
“At present, three tankers” with Russian fuel are on their way to the United States, Russian deputy prime minister Alexander Novak told reporters on Tuesday. A fourth was expected to set off on Wednesday, he added.
The first US-bound tanker with Russian diesel departed last week. According to data from the maritime tracking firm Kpler, it loaded nearly 300,000 barrels of diesel at the Primorsk terminal and was headed to New York.
Dutch broadcaster drops out from Eurovision (again) over Israel's participation
In other news, the Netherlands has dropped (again) from the 2027 Eurovision song contest as public broadcaster NPO reversed its plans to pick up the baton after another broadcaster pulled out in August.
The withdrawal is linked with “sensitivities” over Israel’s participation in the competition, NPO’s media director Jurre Bosman said, acknowledging the issue continues to “elicit various reactions in society and causes discussion and division.”
“Therefore, after consultation with the Board of Broadcasters, the NPO has decided to forgo participation in 2027,” he added.
This is the second time a Dutch broadcaster has dropped out of the competition: in August, the Avrotros, which usually selects the Dutch entry and broadcasts the show, had pulled out, paving the way for NPO to step in.
Ireland and Spain have also declared they will not take part in the 2027 competiton because of Israel’s involvement, and the Czech Republic pulled out over financial constraints. Iceland and Slovenia also didn’t take part.
The 2027 Eurovision song contest will take place in Bulgaria’s Black Sea city of Burgas, after singer Darina Yotova, performing as Dara, won this year’s contest in Austria with “Bangaranga”.
'We have to be ready for a scenario in which the UK and Nato find itself at war with Russia,' UK's Streeting warns
Jakub Krupa
Meanwhile, Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, has warned that Russia’s Vladimir Putin is “testing us and testing Nato’s resolve” as he condemned hybrid threats and “state-sponsored terrorism” from Russia.
Streeting repeated his recent warnings that “we have to be ready for a scenario in which the United Kingdom and the Nato alliance finds itself at war with Russia”. He went on:
Not because we want war – we have no quarrel with the Russian people, and we have no desire for war with Russia; Nato is a defensive alliance – but when Putin gives assurances that he has no intentions to provoke a war with Nato, we are reminded of what he said about Ukraine only days before the invasion.
Speaking in Warsaw alongside Poland’s defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, Streeting stressed Nato is ready “to defend every inch of Nato territory” and will continue its support for Ukraine.
The defence secretary added:
The more ready we are to face against Russia, to defend every inch of Nato territory, the less likely we are to find ourselves in that scenario.
Poland is one of our greatest and certainly our most reliable friend in Europe, and we value and treasure this friendship very much.
The partnership is “not simply about our shared history,” but also “our shared determination that in that contest between freedom and tyranny, the United Kingdom and Poland will not be bystanders.”
He said that UK forces will next month take part in major exercises as part of the multinational force for Ukraine.
Ukraine needs 'real de-escalatory steps' on energy and infrastructure, Zelenskyy says
Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy stressed that “real de-escalatory steps are needed regarding our energy and infrastructure” ahead of critical winter months, as he responded to the reported call with Putin.
In his debrief with Finland’s Stubb and Norway’s Støre, the leaders also discussed preparations for the Abu Dhabi talks next month.
“Finland and Norway, as countries that border Russia, have a particular interest in sound and reliable security arrangements.
We also discussed various formats for our engagement with partners in Europe that could be useful in further supporting diplomacy, our defence, and our shared security.
There must be peace, de-escalation is needed, and Russia must stop dragging out the war.”
Putin blames EU, Nato for 'confrontational policies' and says Russia's interests must be accepted 'in full' in any peace talks
The Kremlin’s readout from Putin’s call with Stubb and Støre offers some more revealing lines from the Russian side, which perhaps show why Frederiksen (and no doubt other leaders) remain deeply sceptical of the idea that these discussions can change anything.
Putin “recalled the root causes” of the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin said, and stressed that any peace settlement could only be reached with “full and unconditional considerations of the legitimate interests of the Russian Federation,” and as we know these tend to be phrased in a very expansive way.
He also blamed the EU and Nato for “confrontational policies,” which in his view “are leading to a prolongation of hostilities.”
The three leaders agreed to keep talking, so expect these issues to come up again.
Danish PM 'very sceptical' about Finnish-Norwegian engagement with Putin on Ukraine
But not everyone seems to be particularly convinced by the joint Finnish-Norwegian initiative.
Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen told the country’s broadcaster DR that she was “very sceptical” about this “independent initiative by Norway and Finland,” stressing “it has not been coordinated with the rest of us.”
“I see no signs that Russia desires peace with Europe – neither in the hybrid warfare taking place every single day, nor in Ukraine, where they are launching fierce and aggressive attacks on a daily basis.
I believe we should keep Europe united, rather than going it alone.”
She told DR that she didn’t know “what they think can be achieved by this.”
“We have previously emphasised – in very clear terms, on behalf of the rest of Europe – whenever others have gone it alone and traveled to Moscow, that it is crucial for us Europeans to stand together. That is something many of us have fought for all these years,” she said.
Stubb confirms 'good phone call' with Zelenskyy as part of 'efforts to find a just and lasting peace' in Ukraine
Finland’s Stubb has just confirmed his call with Zelenskyy.
He said:
“Norwegian PM @jonasgahrstore and I had a good phone call with @ZelenskyyUa.
We discussed our prior call with President Putin. Finland and Norway will continue to support Ukraine, and the efforts to find a just and lasting peace.”
Finland's Stubb and Norway's Støre held 'frank and substantive' call with Putin on Ukraine
Oh, that’s interesting.
There were some rumours making rounds this morning that the Finnish president Alexander Stubb and Norway’s Jonas Gahr Støre, who hosted the US-Ukrainian talks in Oslo last week, may have been active again.
And we now have a formal confirmation: the pair spoke on the phone with Russia’s Vladimir Putinto discuss the latest on Ukraine.
Their call was “a follow-up” to the Oslo meeting, Stubb’s office said in a statement, as the Nordic pair wants to advance their diplomatic efforts to end the Russian war of aggression in Ukraine.
“Finland and Norway border Russia. They are firm supporters of Ukraine. The aim of the call was to convey messages directly regarding future negotiations to help to end the war to President Putin. The call was related to the upcoming meetings to be held in Abu Dhabi,” the statement read.
The trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine, and the US in Abu Dhabi are expected in early November.
“Norway and Finland have always promoted peace and security in our region. The two countries have a shared interest in stability and predictability in the Baltic Sea region and the High North. This was highlighted in the call.”
Curiously, the statement noted that “Stubb and Støre took the call as leaders of their respective countries and did not speak on the behalf of Europe as a whole.”
Reacting after the call, Stubb called the discussions “frank and substantive,” saying that “ending the war requires direct discussions” with Russia.
“The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations. In the call we stressed the importance of de-escalation”, Norway’s Støre added.
The head of Ukraine’s president Zelenskyy’s office, Kyrylo Budanov, has confirmed that the ceasefire in Oleshky is in operation.
“Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets has headed to the site and will be responsible for coordinating the process. We are in constant contact with him.
It is critically important that this mission to rescue our people be carried out successfully and safely. I am sincerely grateful to everyone involved in carrying out and supporting this operation. Every Ukrainian life is priceless.”
Morning opening: Russia, Ukraine begin localised ceasefire to allow aid to Oleshky, but strikes on Kyiv continue
Jakub Krupa
Russia and Ukraine have started a localised ceasefire to allow for a humanitarian operation to begin in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, but Russian strikes continued in other parts of the country, including Kyiv.
Overnight, Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles and more than 280 drones, with at least 15 people injured in Kyiv, with further attacks in the Chernihiv, Chernivtsi, Dnipro, Donetsk, Kharkiv, Kherson, Odesa, Sumy, Vinnytsia, Zaporizhzhia regions.
“A serious escalation in Russia’s operation against our logistics. Almost everywhere, Russia’s targets were the energy sector, logistics, and ordinary urban infrastructure,” Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said.
He added that “the artificial and prolonged delays in the delivery of interceptor packages for Patriot and Nasams systems … are directly helping Russia achieve the objectives of its terrorist campaign.”
“Every such delay means another Russian strike on one facility or another. Unfortunately, strikes are taking place every day. Russia is constantly taking new steps toward escalation.”
I will also be looking at the latest updates from Serbia after Sunday’s parliamentary elections, France after last night’s proposals seeking to end student protests, and elsewhere.
It’s Tuesday, 27 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

articles.title: How will growing US-Ukraine tensions shape the course of the war?
articles.body:
Growing tensions between Washington and Kiev are exposing differences that extend beyond the personal rivalry between US President Donald Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as the White House pursues closer ties with Moscow.
The latest signs of a US-Russia rapprochement emerged last week when US mediator Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Saint Petersburg, with both sides issuing positive statements about renewing peace talks and ending the war in Ukraine.
Yet just hours after the statements, Russia and Ukraine exchanged a deadly barrage of attacks, underscoring the challenges facing efforts to negotiate an end to the conflict.
The growing US-Russia rapprochement, marked by Washington brokering a diesel deal with the Kremlin and lifting most US sanctions on Moscow, has frustrated Zelenskyy, who has recently publicly opposed Washington's softer approach toward Moscow.
Trump has also demanded that Zelenskyy stop targeting Russian refineries.
The disagreements mark a further deterioration in relations that have remained strained since a heated White House meeting in March, when Trump and Zelenskyy engaged in a public shouting match.
Although Zelenskyy subsequently sought common ground with Trump through European mediation, their latest exchanges suggest that the divisions between Washington and Kiev run deeper than disagreements over how to end the war, reflecting increasingly divergent geopolitical priorities and international alignments.
“I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than Putin,” the US president said in a speech last week, underscoring his affinity for the Russian leader, who recently proposed a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Trump to address the war in Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy has shown less hesitation in confronting the US administration, which has long provided Ukraine with weapons, funding and essential intelligence in its war against Russia.
“How can Trump be friends with him? I think that it’s a mistake. It’s his choice again and again,” Zelenskyy said in a recent Financial Times interview, referring to the political rapprochement between Russia and the US.
Rapprochement disrupts Ukrainian resistance
Growing differences between Washington and Kiev, coupled with Trump's rapprochement with Putin, could strengthen Moscow's position both on the battlefield and at the negotiating table, according to experts.
The deepening tensions between the US and Ukraine are “exerting a disruptive influence on the dynamics of the war in Ukraine, affecting both military operations on the ground and the parameters of a potential peace settlement,” Ozgur Korpe, an academic at National Defence University, tells TRT World.
“On the battlefield, uncertainty regarding US aid—compounded by political conditionality—is compelling Ukraine to adopt a more defensive, resource-conserving strategy, while simultaneously granting Russia greater latitude to maintain its offensive tempo and intensify pressure,” he says.
In recent weeks, Ukraine has faced disruptions to US intelligence sharing and Starlink satellite connections, which Kiev believes contributed to its vulnerability during recent deadly Russian missile attacks on the capital.
Shortages of missile interceptors, compounded by delays in US supplies, have further strained Ukraine's air defences.
According to Korpe, Ukraine's predicament reflects a well-documented phenomenon in international relations: when a weaker partner depends heavily on a stronger ally for security, declining support or growing uncertainty over assistance can undermine its willingness and ability to continue fighting.
Since the war began, Kiev has relied heavily on American political, economic, military and intelligence assistance.
Under the Trump administration, however, that support has declined, while the US president has increasingly portrayed Zelenskyy as an obstacle to a potential peace settlement.
Ukraine has sought to offset shortages of American weapons and disruptions to intelligence sharing with support from Europe.
But questions remain over whether countries such as France, the UK and Germany have the military capabilities to replace US assistance.
Domestic priorities
Trump and Zelenskyy have different pledges to their respective national audiences, making compromise increasingly difficult.
While Trump has long pledged to Americans to bring immediate peace to the Russia-Ukraine war, Zelenskyy aims to minimise any territorial concessions to Moscow to keep national support for his presidency strong.
The tensions between Washington and Kiev are “largely a product of US domestic political factors, with the Trump administration facing pressure due to rising energy costs amid prolonged wars in both the Middle East and the Russia/Ukraine conflict,” says Eugene Chausovsky, senior director of analytical development and training at the New Lines Institute.
With the US midterm elections approaching, Trump is seeking ways to ease economic pressures, particularly rising diesel prices and their wider impact on inflation.
“This frames the US agreement with Russia on allowing diesel shipments, as well as Trump’s frustration with Zelensky for Ukraine continuing to target Russian energy and refinery infrastructure at a politically sensitive time,” Chausovsky tells TRT World.
However, experts warn that the diesel deal is unlikely to immediately affect US fuel prices, as European countries continue to enforce their own sanctions on Russia.
Trump’s declaration of an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia also failed, as both sides said they did not sign the agreement.
“Trump frames Ukraine not so much as a front line for the defence of liberal democratic norms, but rather as a costly foreign burden in the context of US domestic politics and a bargaining chip to be used at the negotiating table when striking a ‘grand deal’ with Russia,” Korpe says.
By contrast, Zelenskyy views Ukraine's struggle as existential and closely tied to the country's aspirations to join Western political and military institutions, according to Korpe.
Will Ukraine and the US break up?
Ukraine has long sought closer integration with Western political and military institutions, including NATO and the EU. But deteriorating relations with Washington have raised questions about whether Kiev can keep relying on American support.
Oleg Ignatov, a senior analyst on Russia at the International Crisis Group, says the Trump administration has recently changed its approach to negotiations aimed at ending the war.
“Previously, Washington tried to reach an understanding with Moscow first, then took its proposals to Ukraine and its allies, who rejected them.
“Now the United States is trying to secure support from Ukraine and its European allies first and find out what they are prepared to accept. It would then take those proposals to Putin,” Ignatov tells TRT World.
Last week, US mediators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, met Ukrainian and European leaders in Oslo before Witkoff travelled to Saint Petersburg for further talks with Putin.
“This approach requires Zelenskyy to be clearer about the compromises Ukraine might accept. That is likely to cause friction between Kiev and Washington because their approaches still differ,” Ignatov tells TRT World.
If the US continues to push Zelenskyy to make further concessions to Russia, this approach could “lead to further friction or even conflict between Kiev and Washington,” Ignatov says.
Zelenskyy has insisted that any potential ceasefire must be backed by Western security guarantees without territorial concessions to Russia.
In a recent CNN interview, Zelenskyy maintained that Ukraine “will survive” and “will stay strong” despite tensions with Washington, while rejecting territorial concessions to Russia.
Although some analysts attribute the tensions partly to personal animosity between Trump and Zelenskyy, Korpe argues that the differences run deeper.
“The rift between the two leaders is not merely personal; rather, it is rooted in deeper disagreements regarding the objectives of the war and the vision for a final settlement.”
Korpe says institutions such as the US Congress and the Pentagon, alongside NATO, have helped prevent American support for Ukraine from collapsing entirely.
Nevertheless, “it is fair to say that the crisis of trust between the two leaders is moving distinctly toward a complete ‘break’,” he adds.
Chausovsky, however, offers a different assessment.
While Zelenskyy and the Trump administration remain at odds, he says, “these tensions should not be seen as a sign of a breakup” between Washington and Kiev.
Instead, Chausovsky describes the current friction as “rather a down period in the ebb and flow of their ties amid the protracted conflict with Russia.”
“Greater diplomatic activity can be expected as a result, though any sustainable ceasefire or peace agreement is unlikely to materialise in the short term,” he tells TRT World.

articles.title: Netanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to election
articles.body:
Benjamin Netanyahu has resorted to increasingly alarmist rhetoric and reportedly put pressure on Israel’s military to take action against Iran as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in the polls ahead of Tuesday’s close-run elections.
The Israeli prime minister posted an AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud destroying Tel Aviv, telling Israeli voters to choose him or risk nuclear annihilation.
“Anyone who cares about their own physical existence, that of their family, and their loved ones should have a trembling hand before voting for [the opposition],” he wrote in a social media post about Iran’s nuclear programme.
Israel’s Channel 12 news reported that the prime minister and the armed forces chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, clashed in recent days over a directive to the military which could “potentially spark an immediate conflagration with Iran at a very sensitive juncture”, by provoking a miscalculation by Iran.
Zamir is reported to have requested the directive, the details of which were not specified, to be presented to him in writing.
Netanyahu denied the report, and the defence ministry later denied any intention to carry out military operations against Iran.
On Monday however, CNN reported that Netanyahu had tried to convince Donald Trump to launch a renewed assault on Iran in recent weeks, renewing the war both men started in February.
The report, confirming an earlier account in the Financial Times, said Trump had ruled out any such action until US congressional elections next week.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) issued a statement on Monday that stopped well short of a denial of the press reports. It simply insisted that its decisions were based exclusively on “security, professional, objective and national considerations”.
Netanyahu’s warnings were a marked contrast with his triumphalism in the immediate wake of the wars on Iran that launched last year and this spring.
In March Netanyahu said Israeli and US strikes had destroyed Iran’s ability to enrich uranium and produce ballistic missiles, and in 2025 he claimed a “historic victory” over Iran that would stand for generations.
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s most likely challenger for the prime minister’s job, expressed his confidence in Zamir. “We won’t allow the IDF to be turned into a pawn in Netanyahu’s survival campaign,” said Eisenkot, who is a retired general.
Most polls suggest the mainly centre-right opposition bloc led by Eisenkot is poised to win more seats in Israel’s Knesset than the Netanyahu coalition, but neither would be able to muster the 61 seats necessary for a majority government.
The opposition would most likely be able to gather a majority and topple Netanyahu in coalition with parties representing Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, roughly a fifth of the population. But conservatives inside the Eisenkot bloc have ruled out such a coalition, raising the prospect of a minority government, another round of elections and a possible Netanyahu resurgence.
As the elections drew closer, Netanyahu framed the country’s choice as existential. He told Channel 14, which has acted as his lead cheerleader in the Israeli media: “There is a single fundamental issue here – our existence.”
He described the opposition bloc as the “left” in alliance with Palestinians, and enemies of the country. “We see what is happening in Europe. The alliance between the left and Islam might destroy the state of Israel,” he said.
The main opposition parties are rightwing or centre-right, sharing Netanyahu’s adamant opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state, and who have largely supported the war in Gaza. Some opposition leaders have ruled out any kind of political alliance with Palestinian Israeli parties, who could emerge from the elections holding the balance of power in the Knesset. Palestinians in the occupied territories do not have the vote.
The opposition bloc is held together more by its shared antipathy to Netanyahu, who has dominated the Israeli political scene over the past three decades and veered increasingly towards authoritarianism, seeking to limit the independence of the judiciary and turn the police and Shin Bet internal security service into political tools.
The prime minister is also in the midst of a trial on corruption charges, and his legal jeopardy could increase if he loses his grip on power.
In the closing stages of the campaign, Netanyahu has also emphasised the overt support he enjoys from Donald Trump, who repeated his endorsement on Sunday in a social media post, saying “When you go to the Polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding warrior prime minister!”
The Israeli outlet Walla News reported that this repeat endorsement was a result of relentless pressure from Netanyahu’s office. It is unclear, however, whether Trump’s support will carry any weight with the electorate. The US president’s earlier “total endorsement” on 18 October made no visible difference to the polls.
In one survey, 64% of Israelis questioned said it would not influence their vote, and 17% said it made them less likely to back Netanyahu, against 12% who said it had deepened their resolve to support Netanyahu’s Likud party.
In the closing stages of the closely fought campaign, Netanyahu has also forecast growing financial isolation, saying billions of dollars in annual military aid from the US would dry up soon, and drew a rare public rebuke from the central bank for a repeated claim that Israel could use cryptocurrencies to dodge escalating global sanctions.
“Cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a means to circumvent sanctions,” the Bank of Israel said on Sunday evening. “The right course for the Israeli economy is to maintain economic relations with our primary trading partners and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy.”
Netanyahu had already laid out a forecast for a bleak, isolated future a year ago, when he said Israel might need to become a militarised “super Sparta”, then rowed back again in the face of fierce criticism from a horrified Israeli public.
His return to this rhetoric and the tactics of fear, particularly after unexpected losses for far-right allies in Serbia and Brazil, raised questions about whether the ultimate political survivor may finally be on the ropes.
Few among his allies or enemies expected his government to survive long after 7 October, much less complete its term. But the majority of polls have been clear for more than two years that his current coalition looks set to lose its slim majority.

articles.title: ‘Delays Directly Assist Russia’: Zelensky Slams Slow Delivery of Interceptors
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky criticized delays in the delivery of air defense interceptors for Patriot and NASAMS systems on Tuesday, Oct. 27, saying they directly help Russia carry out its attacks.
“The artificial and prolonged delays in the delivery of interceptor packages for Patriot and NASAMS systems – which have unfortunately been occurring recently – directly assist Russia in achieving the goals of its terrorist campaign,” Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Every such delay results in another Russian strike hitting a target. Sadly, these attacks happen every single day,” he added, calling for stronger pressure on Moscow and timely military assistance to Kyiv.
The overnight attack hit Kyiv, including the Pivdennyi (South) Bridge, as well as energy, logistics, and civilian infrastructure in multiple regions.
At the time, Zelensky said the number of people injured in the Russian strike on a university campus and surrounding area had risen to 12, including five university students and staff. However, per updated reports, the overnight assault resulted in one person killed and 15 others injured.
“While emergency services were assisting people and addressing the aftermath of the initial strike, the Russians launched ballistic missiles again,” Zelensky wrote.
He said Russia had fired 16 ballistic missiles overnight, along with more than 280 drones.
According to Zelensky, Russian strikes were reported in Kyiv, Vinnytsia, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv, Odesa, Chernihiv, Sumy, Donetsk, Kherson, and the Chernivtsi regions.
What Israel’s Election Could Change for Ukraine and Relations With Russia
“In almost every instance, the Russian targets were energy infrastructure, logistics, and civilian urban infrastructure,” he said.
Zelensky stressed that pressure on Russia and concrete support for Ukraine were necessary to change the situation. He thanked those who support Ukraine’s defense and understand the importance of ensuring that military aid arrives on time.
“We must bring peace closer and save lives,” he said.
Ukrainian air defenses shot down or neutralized two Russian Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles and 255 drones during an overnight attack primarily targeting Kyiv, the Air Force reported.
Impacts were recorded at 25 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at 16 locations.
The attack prompted the closure of Kyiv’s South (Pivdennyi) Bridge and disruptions on the Green Line metro. Mayor Vitalii Klitschko released the first photos showing damage to the bridge, which remains closed as specialists assess the damage.
Authorities have not announced when traffic or normal metro service will resume.
In Kyiv, strikes also damaged an administrative building in the Podilskyi district and other non-residential buildings.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has asked the UK, France, Germany, Italy, and Poland to provide 10% of their existing stocks of Patriot and IRIS-T interceptor missiles to help defend against Russian attacks.
Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said Kyiv proposed exchanging the missiles for ammunition already contracted for future delivery. Ukraine also needs additional man-portable air defense systems (MANPADS).
Following talks in Paris, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said European partners had prepared winter aid packages for Ukraine and were working with Kyiv to develop an air defense system.
On Monday, Oct. 26, Zelensky said Ukraine had waited nearly a month for US approval of Patriot and NASAMS missiles and would raise the issue with Washington again.
He said Ukraine received only 24 Patriot interceptors from the US over 90 days, despite needing around 350 per month, and has sought 300 interceptors from European partners for winter.
