articles.title: Russian Ballistic Missiles Hit Kyiv University Area, Killing 1, Wounding 10
articles.body:
Russian ballistic missiles struck a university campus and surrounding residential areas in Kyiv late Monday, Oct. 26, killing at least one person and injuring over 10 others, most of them students, as emergency crews searched damaged buildings for people feared trapped under rubble.
The strikes hit the grounds of a university near Kyoto Park and Lisova metro station on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, damaging student dormitories, residential buildings, and medical facilities.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said nine of the wounded were hospitalized, including three in serious condition.
President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that further strikes were possible as Russian Shahed drone attacks continued against the capital and other Ukrainian cities.
“There is extensive damage, and there are also reports that people may be trapped under the rubble,” Zelensky wrote on social media.
The Ukrainian leader stressed that the missiles struck crowded civilian areas where, he said, there were no military facilities nearby.
“Unfortunately, there may be more strikes coming,” Zelensky added.
At 8:30 a.m. on Tuesday, the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) reported that the number of casualties had risen to 15.
“Overnight, the enemy attacked the capital with ballistic missiles and [unmanned aerial vehicles] UAVs. As a result of the Russian Federation’s terrorist actions, damage has been recorded in three districts of Kyiv,” the report reads.
Zelensky Outlines Three Security Options as US Pushes for November Talks With Russia
Of the 15 casualties, 12 have been hospitalized.
According to the State Emergency Service (DSNS), two fires broke out in non-residential buildings in the Obolonskyi district. Rescuers have extinguished both fires. Two casualties were reported in the district.
In the Holosiivskyi district, the Russian attack damaged transport infrastructure.
University campus and student dormitories damaged
The university affected by the attack was identified as the State University of Trade and Economics (SUTE), located on Kyoto Street in Kyiv’s Desnianskyi district.
The institution, founded in 1946, is one of the capital’s major public universities, with more than 15,000 students across six faculties, according to its official profile.
The university specializes in economics, international trade, finance, law, information technology, and management.
Russia’s ballistic strike landed near a university dormitory, shattering windows and injuring residents, according to Klitschko.
The mayor initially reported that a 20-year-old woman was hospitalized following the strike near the dormitory.
In a subsequent update, Klitschko said most of the 10 people injured in the attack were students living in university accommodation. Nine were taken to hospital.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service reported damage to university buildings, dormitories and nearby residential properties.
KMVA also reported damage to a school building in the Desnianskyi district.
A paramedic and an emergency medical technician suffered injuries after their ambulance came under fire in the Desnianskyi district, according to the mayor. Their injuries were not considered critical.
A strike near Lisova metro station also set a private vehicle on fire, while nearby residential infrastructure sustained damage.
In the Dniprovskyi district, a three-story non-residential building was partially destroyed, with emergency workers discovering the body of one person in its basement, according to the State Emergency Service.
The destruction extended across residential, educational and medical facilities in the two districts.
Zelensky urges allies to accelerate air defense deliveries
Zelensky renewed his call for faster deliveries of Western air defense systems and ammunition, warning that delays were leaving Ukrainian cities vulnerable to further Russian missile strikes.
He said Ukraine continued to face a constant threat from ballistic missiles that could strike populated areas with little warning.
Under such circumstances, he argued, “artificial delays in providing air defense to Ukraine help terror.”
The president called for political agreements on defense assistance to be implemented promptly, stressing that Ukraine needed sufficient weapons not only to intercept incoming missiles but also to destroy Russian launchers.
The latest attack came amid an intensified Russian missile and drone campaign against Ukraine, with Kyiv’s residential neighborhoods, transport facilities, and civilian infrastructure repeatedly affected.

articles.title: Russian ballistic missiles hit a Kyiv university campus, then return before dawn for the Southern Bridge again
articles.body:
Russia attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles and drones in two waves, killing one person, injuring civilians, and damaging university dormitories and apartment blocks, the city military administration said. Russian strikes also killed two people in Kharkiv on the evening of 26 October and wounded civilians in four other oblasts overnight. Daytime attacks on 26 October killed people in Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk, and Kharkiv oblasts.
Russia's war against Ukraine grinds on along the front, where on 26 October alone Russian forces dropped 247 guided bombs and used 9,679 kamikaze drones, the General Staff reported. Behind the front, Russian missiles and drones keep hitting Ukrainian cities, while Washington presses Kyiv rather than Moscow. Ukraine was reportedly told to spare Russian refineries or lose US intelligence and arms. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused US President Donald Trump of trying to pressure Ukraine into capitulating, and a Ukrainian diplomat argues that Trump treats Ukraine as the weak link to be squeezed.
Two ballistic waves hit a Kyiv campus, the center, and the Southern Bridge
Shortly after 22:00 on 26 October, Russian missiles hit near a metro station in Kyiv's left-bank Desnianskyi district, Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported. An ambulance crew that had arrived at a call came under fire, and two medics were injured.
The missiles struck the grounds of one of Kyiv's universities, its campus, Kyoto Park, nearby homes, and the area beside a metro station, Zelenskyy wrote. “There is no military facility nearby,” he said.
In Dniprovskyi district, the blast wave blew out windows in a medical facility's intensive care unit, Klitschko said. A three-story non-residential building in the district partly collapsed.
The evening strike also damaged the metro between two left-bank stations and the exits of Lisova station, Klitschko said.
Kyiv gets no warning of the first of two Russian ballistic waves, hours after Zelenskyy said US alerts were back
A second wave followed before dawn on 27 October. Missiles hit an administrative building in Podilskyi district, Klitschko reported, and at 05:04 he said Russia had hit the Southern (Pivdennyi) Bridge and the metro infrastructure on it.
Police closed the bridge to traffic, and green-line trains stopped crossing it. Russian strikes had already damaged metro infrastructure on the same bridge on 22 October.
The overnight attack set two non-residential buildings on fire in Obolonskyi district, and two more people were injured.
By morning, a 46-year-old woman was dead and 15 people were injured, among them dormitory residents and two medics, the Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office said. Prosecutors counted at least 12 damaged apartment blocks, as well as a burns center, a shopping mall, and a tram.
Kyiv was the main target of the night, the Air Force said, as Russia launched Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles and 280 drones. Air defenses downed two of the missiles and 255 drones.
Zelenskyy put the night's total at 16 ballistic missiles and called the attack “a serious escalation in the Russian operation against our logistics.” He blamed delays in deliveries of interceptors for Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems.
“Artificial and lengthy delays in the delivery of interceptor packages for Patriots and NASAMS, which unfortunately have been happening lately, directly help Russia achieve the goals of its terrorist campaign. Every such delay is a new Russian hit on one target or another.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy
Russian strikes kill two in Kharkiv and wound civilians across Ukraine
Russian strikes on Kharkiv's Novobavarskyi district on the evening of 26 October killed two men and injured four people, including a 17-year-old girl, oblast head Oleh Syniehubov said. On the morning of 27 October, a Russian missile hit Izium, damaging eight houses.
In Zaporizhzhia, a Russian strike on a gas station wounded two people, and a later strike on a car wounded a 17-year-old boy, the oblast administration said. In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Russian drones and aerial bombs injured three women in Synelnykove district overnight.
In Chernihiv Oblast, Russian attacks set homes on fire and injured six people, including a child, the oblast administration said. In Chernivtsi Oblast, a drone attack damaged an energy facility, cutting power until 02:15 and injuring two security guards, oblast head Ruslan Osypenko said. Russian attacks have also critically damaged electrical equipment in northern Khmelnytskyi Oblast, the regional power company said.
Over the past day, Russian attacks killed civilians in Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk, and Kharkiv oblasts
On 26 October, Russian attacks killed three people in Donetsk Oblast and wounded 22, oblast head Vadym Filashkin said. His breakdown puts 16 of the wounded in Yasnohirka, where Russian aircraft dropped guided bombs. A Russian drone strike on Pavlohrad killed one person and wounded seven, and a drone killed a woman in Shevchenkove, Kharkiv Oblast. In Kherson, a Russian drone hit a health facility and wounded a nurse. Most of Konotop in Sumy Oblast has been without power since Russian strikes on 24 October, with no forecast for its return, the mayor said.
Patriot systems are the only ones in Ukraine that reliably stop Russia's Iskander-M ballistic missiles, and their missiles have waited almost a month for a US signature. Every week of that wait leaves cities like Kyiv facing waves like this one with fewer interceptors, which is why Kyiv is also asking Lockheed Martin directly for more.
Read also
- 1,125 Kyiv residents injured in Russian attacks since the start of 2026, more than a third of them in five weeks from late August, Kyiv health chief says
- No warning, capped Starlink, unsigned Patriots: Zelenskyy lists US holds to senators as Kyiv reads them as pressure
- Russian drone cuts down unique energy line tower over Dnipro River in Kyiv. It can’t be rebuilt, and world is queuing for more power equipment

articles.title: Russian Commander Complains NATO Testing Drones on Ukraine’s Front Line
articles.body:
In an interview with Russia’s state news agency TASS on Tuesday, Oct. 27 the commander of Moscow’s Akhmat special forces unit, Lt. Gen. Apti Alaudinov complained that NATO nations were using the war in Ukraine to test drone technology in combat against Russia.
He commented that large numbers of Western manufactured unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV) were being encountered: “We see that drones manufactured in all these countries, which are members of the NATO alliance, are being tested against us on the line of engagement.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Alaudinov claimed that these included drones of every type, capability and operational ranges. According to him, this not only included first-person view (FPV) drones used to attack Russian forces and equipment on the front line but also included long-range UAVs that were being used to carry out deep strikes against towns, cities and infrastructure inside Russia.
The West learning from Ukraine’s experience of drone warfare – a two-way street
In March 2022, in the earliest days of the war, the US Council on Foreign relations commented on how Ukraine relied on drones sourced from Turkey, the Bayraktar TB2, as a means of disrupting Russian tank columns on their march towards Kyiv. Their appearance on the battlefield seemed at first to be a game changer, but it was not long before their vulnerability was exploited by Moscow’s air defenses.
However, the value of drones in taking the war to the enemy and the need for countermeasures was soon appreciated by both sides which led to the battlefield dominance UAVs currently enjoy.
What Israel’s Election Could Change for Ukraine and Relations With Russia
Recent statements by Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense and reports in the Western mainstream and social media seem to partially confirm Alaudinov’s assertions. Ukraine is cooperating with both government and commercial drone-related programs, not only using “attack” and surveillance drones but also to develop counter-drone technology and tactics.
A July report by the Ministry of Defense explained how it was working with NATO’s Allied Command Transformation (ACT) agency using its battlefield experience to support NATO in developing ways to combat drones. The report says this shows that “Ukraine is not only receiving support from its partners but is also actively shaping their approaches to modern warfare.”
On Monday the US publication The Hill reported on comments made by US Air Force Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich, SACEUR, at a meeting in Poland. This followed on from an earlier report by Bloomberg on plans to use artificial intelligence (AI) enhanced drones to defend the alliance. The general laid out a possible strategy in the event of an attack by Russia, the concept of “blunt, block and break.” The articles suggested that the mass use of UAVs would be key to the success of Grynkewich’s plan and suggested that virtually every military was developing UAV-based concepts supplemented with AI for warfighting.
A week ago, the Wall Street Journal reported on how Ukraine’s “Kill Zone” was being used to test and develop the use of AI in drones. This followed a report in the defense issues website the Defense Post that discussed how Ukraine had been deploying AI tools developed in the NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Centre (JATEC) to both plan and control its UAV operations and to predict Russian drone activity. It said a prototype system was undergoing real-time validation by Ukrainian forces.
CBS reported in September that Washington and Kyiv were in the process of agreeing on a policy that would allow the two countries to expand the testing and production of Ukrainian defense technology in the US. It was given new impetus by the use of Iranian drones against US forces in the Middle East.
The report cites experts saying the experience gained by Ukraine in developing drone software and operations, as well as the speed with which it could adapt to battlefield changes, were likely to prove invaluable to the use of drones by the US and its allies.
Deborah Fairlamb, partner in a US venture capital firm that is investing in Ukrainian defense technology, told CBS: “The West needs to start understanding better is that it’s not just about having the tech. It’s about how the tech is used. And this is where Ukraine’s knowledge, skills, experience really need to be transmitted.”
In a separate report on its YouTube channel in July, CBS reported on how Ukraine was deploying US drone technology, such as the “Shield AI” V-Bat vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) reconnaissance and targeting UAV, to support long-range strikes into Russia.

articles.title: Eyes on Israel elections, Iran says US 'not serious' on talks
articles.body:
Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey, states of the newly established Mecca Pact, met with Iran's president and security chief in Tehran, with both sides seeking to continue diplomacy
Voters in Israel head to the polls in the first general vote since the start of the genocidal war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023
The war in Yemen rages, with the Saudi-led coalition intercepting Houthi ballistic missiles and Houthi-affiliated media reported that Yemeni government forces launched air strikes in Taiz province
Israeli attacks continue on Gaza, occupied West Bank, south Lebanon and southern Syria
And so we continue our live coverage of the day...
Israeli voter turnout stood at 44.9% as of 2 p.m., according to the Central Elections Committee.
It is the highest turnout at this hour since hourly numbers have been records, in 1973, with over three million people having voted. The previous record at 2 p.m. was in 1988, 2.7 percent points less than in 2026.
Iran army: oil tanker on fire after hitting mines in Hormuz
The Iranian army on Tuesday said an oil tanker hit mines and caught fire while attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz via a route not authorised by Tehran.
"A few hours ago, an oil tanker in breach of regulations, having switched off its tracking systems and attempted to cross a prohibited and dangerous area east of the Strait of Hormuz, struck naval mines, causing damage and a fire," the army said in a statement carried by the official IRNA news agency.
Saudi crown prince reviews Tehran talks with cabinet
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman chaired a meeting in Riyadh Tuesday where he and his council of ministers reviewed talks held in Tehran with the Mecca alliance a day earlier, state media reported.
"The council reviewed the substance of the talks held between the countries party to the Mecca Common Defence Agreement and senior officials of the Islamic Republic of Iran, reaffirming Saudi Arabia's commitment to establishing security and stability," read a statement released by state media.
Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iranian senior leaders in Tehran on Monday on the Middle East war, with Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei later calling the discussions "very good".
Police arrest man threatening Israel left-wing leader
Police on Tuesday arrested a man with a knife who moved threateningly towards Yair Golan, leader of Israel's main left-wing party, as he mobilised voters in Tel Aviv on election day, his party said.
"Incitement and violence will not intimidate us," Golan said in a statement, blaming the incident on the "poison machine" of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has sharply attacked the left in his campaign.
Golan was trying to get out the vote at a park in Tel Aviv when a stranger approached him in a threatening manner, said his party, The Democrats.
When Golan's security guards blocked the man, a large knife fell out of his clothing, the party added. The security guards then arrested him.
Qatar's emir meets Iran’s president at Moscow summit
Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani met with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Moscow, according to Iran’s state news agency IRNA.
On the sidelines of the 8th summit of heads of state of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum, the two leaders discussed ways to develop bilateral relations and strengthen cooperation in the energy sector, including gas, IRNA said.
The two leaders also reviewed the relationship status between Tehran and Doha, and emphasised the importance of expanding political and economic ties, IRNA added.
Houthis: targeted Saudi oil refinery with ballistic missile
Yemen's Houthis on Tuesday said they targeted Saudi Arabia's biggest oil refinery with a ballistic missile, following weeks of disruptive attacks against the world's top crude exporter.
"The Yemeni Armed Forces were able to target the Ras Tanura refinery in the Eastern Province with a ballistic missile," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree posted on X, saying the strike caused "massive fires".
In recent weeks, Yemen's Houthis have been striking Saudi Arabia. [Getty]
Israel voter turnout at 31.5% as of noon, highest since 1973
Voter turnout in Israel's election stood at 31.5% as of noon local, according to the Central Elections Committee, up from 28.4% at the same time in the 2022 election.
It is the highest turnout at this hour since 1973, in the first election held after the war.
10 factors that could decide the vote in Israel's elections
From Arab voter turnout and ultra-Orthodox divisions to youth participation and coalition negotiations, there are 10 main factors that could fundamentally shape Israel's election results.
Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich warned that the high voter turnout by the 1948 Palestinan and Arab community, as well as from left-wing strongholds, may affect the election results.
He called on voters to vote for right-wing parties that guarantee exceeding the electoral threshold, and not to waste their votes on right-wing parties that fall below it.
Israeli elections offer scant hope of change for Gaza
According Israeli media, citing The Washington Post, US President Donald Trump is pressing for the formation of a coalition that would include Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot.
The Washington Post reported that Netanyahu has been engaging with figures in the US administration and Europe, presenting himself as the ideal partner in confronting Iran.
As part of these discreet contacts, Netanyahu ndicated that if a broad government were formed with Eisenkot, he would exclude Itamar Ben-Gvir and his party from the coalition.
The move aligns with an initiative being promoted by the US administration to establish a regional coalition based on the Abraham Accords, with particular emphasis on Saudi Arabia.
The American proposal includes a rotating premiership arrangement under which Netanyahu would serve for approximately two years, end the wars and advance diplomatic agreements before retiring from political life.
Sources in the United States claimed that Israeli President Isaac Herzog is involved in the discussions and could potentially grant Netanyahu a pardon, despite explicit denials from the president's office.
Two charged in UK with security offences on airbase plot
UK anti-terrorism police said Tuesday that two men have been charged with national security offences after an incident last month at a British airbase used by the United States.
The head of National Counter Terrorism Policing, Laurence Taylor, said two British nationals have been charged: one with assisting a foreign intelligence service, believed to be in Iran, and another with entering a prohibited place for a purpose "prejudicial" to the UK.
Voter turnout in the first three hours of Israel's pivotal general election stood at 16.68 percent, the Central Elections Committee said on Tuesday, the highest at this stage of the vote since 1981.
"By 10 am, more than 1,200,000 Israelis had voted. The nationwide voter turnout stands at 16.68 percent," Dean Livne, acting director general of the committee, said in a televised statement.
Adalah: Shortage of Arabic-language ballots reported
The New Arab's correspondent Naif Zidane repors that since the polls opened this morning, the Adalah Centre—the Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel—has received reports from voters and observers indicating that Arabic-language ballots were not available in many polling stations. These reports came from several Arab towns including: Baqa al-Gharbiyye, Haifa, Nazareth, I'billin, I'boun, Shefa-'Amr, and Nof HaGalil.
Following these reports, Adalah sent an urgent letter to the Chair of the Central Elections Committee, calling for the defect to be corrected immediately by promptly supplying Arabic-language ballots to all stations experiencing shortages and issuing clear instructions to polling committees.
What occurred constitutes an infringement on Arab citizens' right to vote equally and accessibly. Arabic is the mother tongue of hundreds of thousands of voters, and providing ballots in Arabic is an essential condition for conducting fair and legitimate elections.
China is highly concerned about conflicts in the Middle East and surrounding regions and Beijing will send an envoy to the relevant countries in the near future, foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a daily press conference on Tuesday.
Guo called on related parties to resolve differences through dialogue and negotiation and also expressed concerns about the spillover and transmitting of the Middle East conflict to the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea region.
"China will soon send a special envoy to visit countries in the regions to strengthen communication with relevant parties, promote contact and dialogue, help ease tensions and prevent the situation from deteriorating further," Guo said.
Jordan claims strikes on Syria killed over 20 IS militants
Jordan said its air force killed more than 20 Islamic State militants in strikes on southern Syria on Monday night.
The attacks—which the kingdom said on Monday were conducted in coordination with Damascus—avoided known civilian areas, Jordan's Government Communication Minister, Mohammed al-Momani, said on X on Tuesday.
Syrian authorities had said the Jordanian strikes killed seven people, including three children and a woman, in a preliminary report issued on Monday night.
As a Palestinian, liberation is a right, not a plea
Green MPs attacking the passing of the Zionism is racism motion undermine both the party's democratic process and Palestinian voices, writes Amro Tabari.
Houthi official told the media that Egypt's plan to military support Saudi Arabia would be considered a 'declaration of war' by the Iran-backed group in Yemen.
Across the political spectrum, Israel has abandoned any pretence of ending the occupation, halting settlements, or allowing Palestinian statehood, writes Kate McMahon.
Iran's security chief said on Monday he held "very good discussions" with the three member nations of the Mecca defence pact, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, after their first meeting in Tehran.
"Very good discussions took place between us," Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told state television after the meeting with top officials from the three countries. "I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region... I sensed a very positive atmosphere in the discussions among the gentlemen."
The meeting, proposed by Pakistan, brought together senior officials from the three countries and Iran for talks in the Iranian capital.
Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry said earlier Monday that the meeting aimed to "de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis".
Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan's army chief General Asim Munir and Turkey's intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin represented their countries at the talks. They also met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.
Rezaei said the four parties agreed that regional security should be ensured by countries in the region rather than outside powers.
"The outcomes we agreed on were that security in the region where we live should be endogenous, meaning it should be achieved by the countries themselves," he said.
"We must prevent any kind of foreign intervention in this region," he added.

articles.title: Indian and Russian forces deploy drones and robotic systems in simulated combat
articles.body:
Indian and Russian forces deploy drones and robotic systems in simulated combat
Indian and Russian troops have finished up the INDRA-2026 military exercises in Chelyabinsk Region. During simulated combat, they worked with drones, artillery, tanks, and robotic systems, making use of real-world battlefield experience.
The ground phase of the exercise ended on Friday after ten days at a Russian Central Military District training ground, Russia’s Defense Ministry said.
The final operation simulated the enemy occupying a settlement and establishing defensive positions. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and ground-based robotic systems carried out reconnaissance before artillery units and strike drones targeted mock command posts, weapons positions, and supply depots, clearing the way for a joint assault.
The joint contingents then advanced under cover from tanks, air defense systems, mobile fire teams, and first-person-view (FPV) drone interceptors. The forces practiced securing the settlement and pursuing the retreating enemy, completing the ground exercise.
The October 14-23 drills focused on joint command and control and coordinating operations against armed groups. The Russian contingent consisted primarily of personnel from the Central Military District’s 90th Guards Tank Division.
💥🇮🇳🇷🇺 Total Annihilation: India, Russia Unleash Drones, Tanks & Assault Teams In Massive INDRA-2026 Drills The joint contingents unleashed relentless firepower to encircle and wipe out simulated fortified enemy positions. 📹 🇷🇺 MoD https://t.co/gz4zLkZnzk
— RT_India (@RT_India_news) October 24, 2026
The exercise incorporated lessons from recent armed conflicts to improve combat readiness and coordination between tactical units, Central Military District combat training chief Sergei Pimenkov said at the closing ceremony.
”All assigned tasks were accomplished and the objectives achieved during the joint training,” he said.
For the air component of the exercise, Russian and Indian aircrews practiced coordinated missions using Su-30SM fighter jets, including engaging low-flying targets and maneuvering combat at medium and low altitudes. Mi-8 helicopter crews rehearsed special forces deployments and search-and-rescue operations.
The naval component concluded earlier in the Sea of Japan, where the Indian frigate INS Sahyadri and the Russian corvette Aldar Tsydenzhapov conducted live-fire artillery exercises, counter-drone operations, and a simulated mission to rescue a hijacked civilian vessel. The INS Sahyadri departed Vladivostok on October 20 following the naval exercise, India’s Defense Ministry said.
”We have seen how professionally the Russian armed forces are working,” Indian Brigadier Shubhanshu Kamatnurkar told RT. He said the Indian troops were able to gain from the Russians' frontline combat experience during the exercise.
The INDRA exercises are part of regular military cooperation between India and Russia.

articles.title: U.S. Air Force puts its first hypersonic missile into production
articles.body:
- The U.S. Air Force awarded Lockheed Martin a $694 million contract to produce and field the ARRW hypersonic missile.
- The service withheld quantities and delivery dates, three years after it had planned to cancel the weapon without production buys.
The U.S. Air Force has put its first hypersonic weapon into production, awarding Lockheed Martin a $694 million contract on Sept. 29 to build and field the AGM-183A Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon, or ARRW, a missile the service had planned to abandon just three years ago, the Department of the Air Force announced on Oct. 26.
The service withheld how many missiles the contract covers and when deliveries will begin, citing operational security, but said the award formally moves the weapon out of prototyping and flight testing and into production. The contract was placed through the Department of War’s Enterprise-Wide Agile Acquisition Contract.
ARRW is a boost-glide weapon that rides a solid-fuel rocket booster to more than five times the speed of sound, about 6,100 km/h (3,800 mph), before releasing a glide vehicle that maneuvers toward its target, which makes it far harder to track and intercept than a conventional ballistic missile. The U.S. Air Force says it will let aircraft strike time-sensitive, heavily defended and high-value targets from long range, outside the reach of enemy air defenses.
“This is a turning point in our advanced weapons roadmap. By moving ARRW from test to production, we’re providing our combatant commanders with a credible, high-speed strike weapon capable of penetrating the most advanced anti-access and area-denial systems,” said Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink.
The missile is too large for most fighters and will initially be carried by the B-52 Stratofortress bomber, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported, and it has also reportedly been tested on the B-1.
“Fielding ARRW enhances our ability to hold targets at risk anywhere around the world. This hypersonic weapon provides the Joint Force a flexible and rapid response option for highly contested environments,” said Chief of Staff of the Air Force Gen. Ken Wilsbach.
The production decision caps a troubled development history. Lockheed won the design contract in 2018, but the first three flight tests starting in 2021 failed before the missile flew successfully in May 2022, and in March 2023 the service’s then top acquisition official, Andrew Hunter, said the program would end without any production buys as the U.S. Air Force shifted its focus to the smaller Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile. The service reversed course in 2025, when then-Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin told Congress the U.S. Air Force would buy ARRW.
The program received $362 million in fiscal 2026, and the U.S. Air Force has requested $452 million for production in fiscal 2027, although that request is stalled in Congress while the Pentagon operates under a continuing resolution at 2026 funding levels. Budget plans call for $556 million to $621 million a year for ARRW procurement from 2028 to 2031, with missile quantities marked as controlled unclassified information.

articles.title: Kiev makes new demand for European interceptors
articles.body:
Kiev makes new demand for European interceptors
Ukraine has asked five European nations to release 10% of their interceptor missile stockpiles to ease the shortage of air defense ammunition.
Defense Minister Evgeny Khmara presented the proposal by video on Monday to his counterparts from France, Germany, Italy, and the UK, and Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski, who met in Paris. He said their Patriot and IRIS-T stocks can be replenished from future deliveries contracted for Ukraine with foreign funding.
Khmara floated a similar proposal for advance deliveries of Patriots last month. Kiev also accused Washington of delaying deliveries of the interceptors. US officials cited the competing military needs of their own forces and denied any change in policy toward Ukraine.
The five countries’ joint statement made no commitment to supply additional interceptors, though they reiterated their support for Ukraine “by all available means – politically, militarily and financially.”
Poland and the Netherlands have said they have no Patriot missiles to spare; Greece has warned that aid must not undermine its own defenses. Germany, a key donor, has pledged additional older PAC-2 interceptors from its military stocks. Other European countries have reportedly held back PAC-3 missiles to preserve their own reserves.
The shortage comes amid an escalating exchange of long-range strikes. Kiev intensified drone attacks on Russian oil refineries and retail warehouses over the summer in what Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky called a “40-day pressure campaign.” Russia has said its increased strikes on Ukrainian targets are retaliation. Ukrainian forces are struggling to intercept Russian ballistic missiles and faster, jet-powered long-range drones.
Kiev is also seeking additional financial support after overspending this year. Zelensky has asked European donors for at least €70 billion ($78 billion) to cover military and budget needs; Western governments are struggling to agree on how to finance additional aid.
The EU, which borrowed €90 billion ($100 billion) last year to prop up the government in Kiev for 2026-2027, is facing tensions among member states, with the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Slovakia saying they won’t take part in a potential new loan proposed by the European Commission.

articles.title: Helsing Developed the Contra Autonomous AI-Controlled Air Defense System
articles.body:
Helsing has developed the Contra autonomous AI-controlled air defense system, which independently controls interceptors.
Militarnyi reported this based on the company’s presentation, which took place at its new office in Berlin.
Contra enables the simultaneous detection and engagement of hundreds or thousands of air targets—including drones and missiles. To do this, the system integrates sensor and weapons data into a unified air picture and autonomously decides on target interception while maintaining human oversight.
The system was designed from the outset to integrate third-party equipment. Specifically, this includes other interceptors, laser systems for countering UAVs, anti-drone cannons, and net-based interception systems.
“Contra is capable of defending against massive attacks, missiles, and the latest generation of attack drones. It is a single system for various tasks, independent of the type of equipment,” the company states.
As part of the Contra project, Helsing has developed two high-speed interceptors: the AD-1 Inferno, powered by a jet engine, and the AD-2 Ambush, powered by a solid-fuel rocket engine.
“They are designed to outperform even the fastest threats posed by jet-powered drones and cruise missiles in terms of speed and effectiveness,” the company says.
Helsing has already signed a contract to supply Contra, while the AD-1 and AD-2 interceptors are currently undergoing testing.
Contra is powered by Altra—Helsing’s military artificial intelligence, command, and control platform.
Altra integrates data from radar, electro-optical, infrared, and acoustic sensors from various manufacturers via open, published interfaces. The platform also enables interoperability with the SitaWare system and national combat management systems.
Contra is designed to operate even under conditions of electronic warfare, loss of communication channels, and failure of individual system components.
The AD-1 is a jet-powered interceptor designed to fill gaps in defense capabilities. It is intended for situations where threats outmatch electric interceptors in flight performance and traditional missile systems are too expensive for widespread use.
The Inferno launches immediately upon target detection and receives guidance commands during the cruise phase from the Contra system’s ground-based radar stations.
The interceptor can remain airborne for extended periods in standby mode, operate as part of a swarm, and re-engage targets in flight.
The AD-1 is designed for mass production in Europe under European control. According to the developers’ concept, it is intended to provide a more favorable cost-to-effect ratio for the defending side in terms of weapons and interception capabilities. The AD-1 integrates into the Contra system at the basic architecture level.
The AD-2 is an interceptor equipped with a solid-fuel rocket engine, designed to rapidly intercept targets in the upper threat range.
It can destroy high-speed, single-use strike drones flying at high altitudes, as well as subsonic cruise missiles beyond the AD-1’s range.
The Ambush is designed for mass production. This enables defense forces to maintain intensive interception of large numbers of targets without relying on a single production line.
The AD-2 integrates with Contra at the system’s basic architecture level and receives guidance commands during the cruise phase from Contra’s ground-based radar stations.
Most affordable homing heads use electro-optical (EO) or infrared (IR) cameras.
Electro-optical cameras are unable to reliably track targets in the dark, and both types of cameras may perform poorly in cloudy or foggy weather.
According to the developers, the AD-1 and AD-2 radar homing heads overcome these limitations. They are also built with standard, commercially available components.
AI optimizes the interceptor’s flight path to maximize the probability of a successful hit.

articles.title: Russia’s Jet Shaheds Are Scaling Fast—Helsing Just Unveiled an AI Air Defense Built to Hunt Them
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Jet Shaheds Are Scaling Fast—Helsing Just Unveiled an AI Air Defense Built to Hunt Them
Europe’s answer to Russia’s growing jet-drone arsenal is taking shape around a simple idea: use AI to coordinate mass interceptions, then kill fast threats with cheaper missiles instead of burning through million-euro air-defense rounds.
European defense technology company Helsing has unveiled Contra, a new AI-controlled air-defense system built to counter large-scale drone and missile attacks, alongside two new interceptors designed to chase down fast jet-powered UAVs and cruise missiles, according to a press releaseHelsing shared with UNITED24 Media on October 26.
The system is particularly relevant to Ukraine, which is already facing a growing Russian arsenal of jet-powered Geran drones.
Helsing says recent intelligence assessments indicate Russia has sharply increased production of Geran-4 and Geran-5 systems, with output reportedly reaching as many as 4,000 units per month while Moscow expands the number of launch sites.
Built for the jet-Shahed problem
Contra is designed for exactly that kind of saturation threat.
According to Helsing, the system can detect and coordinate engagements against hundreds or even thousands of incoming drones and missiles at the same time by combining multiple sensors and weapons into a single air picture. Its sensor architecture can include radar, electro-optical, infrared, and acoustic systems, while the Altra command-and-control platform keeps human operators in control of targeting priorities and decisions.
The architecture is also intended to remain functional under battlefield disruption, including jamming, broken communications links, and the loss of individual nodes.
For Ukraine, that matters because Russia’s newer jet-powered Geran variants are substantially faster than conventional Shahed-type drones, increasing the pressure on both interceptor drones and traditional surface-to-air missile systems.
Two new interceptors for two different threats
At the center of Contra are two Helsing-developed interceptors.
The AD-1 Inferno is a jet-powered interceptor intended to fill the gap between slower electric or propeller-driven drone interceptors and traditional missiles that are too expensive to fire in large numbers. Helsing says AD-1 can loiter after launch, operate in swarms, and re-engage targets in flight while receiving midcourse updates from Contra ground radars.
Company specifications list a maximum speed above 700 km/h and an operating altitude exceeding 9,000 meters.
The AD-2 Ambush, meanwhile, uses a solid rocket motor and is intended for faster and higher-flying threats. Helsing says it is designed to defeat high-speed one-way drones and subsonic cruise missiles beyond AD-1’s reach.
In its announcement, Helsing said AD-2 can reach roughly Mach 2.5 and engage targets beyond 20 kilometers.
Both interceptors use onboard radar seekers for terminal guidance, allowing them to operate in darkness, cloud, and fog—conditions where cheaper optical or infrared seekers can struggle. Helsing’s technical brief specifically emphasizes that the radar seekers are intended to maintain performance when visibility is poor.
Built for mass attacks, not one-off shots
Helsing is positioning Contra as more than a closed missile system.
The architecture is designed to integrate third-party weapons—including other interceptors, anti-drone lasers, guns, and even net-based systems—within days.
That would allow operators to choose different weapons for different targets rather than firing an expensive missile at every incoming drone.
The same command architecture is intended to protect population centers, borders, military bases, and maneuvering forces, with the sensor and weapon mix changing depending on the mission.
Helsing says both AD-1 and AD-2 are intended for mass production through separate European supply chains, reducing dependence on a single production line.
Niklas Köhler, Helsing co-founder and president, framed the system around the cost problem now confronting Ukraine and Europe.
“Contra ends the air defence dilemma: slow fair-weather drones, or million-euro missiles fired at cheap, mass-produced targets. Our AI links existing sensors and effectors in real time and adds our interceptors, AD-1 and AD-2. With jet and rocket propulsion, a low-cost all-weather radar seeker, and two independent European supply chains, they deliver autonomous fire superiority up to ten kilometres high—affordable and at industrial scale,” he said.
Ukraine already fighting the threat Contra was built for
For Ukraine, that dilemma is no longer theoretical.
Russia is moving beyond slower propeller-driven Shahed-type drones toward faster jet-powered systems such as the Geran-4 and Geran-5, forcing Ukraine to field increasingly fast interceptor drones, fighter aircraft, surface-to-air missiles, and other layers of defense.
The challenge is not simply destroying one fast drone, but doing so repeatedly during mass attacks without exhausting expensive interceptor stocks.
Contra is Helsing’s attempt to turn those different defensive layers into one coordinated network—using AI to manage the air picture while cheaper, mass-produced interceptors take on threats that would otherwise consume far more expensive missiles.
If Russia continues scaling jet-powered drone production at the rate Helsing describes, that cost equation could become one of the defining problems for both Ukrainian and European air defense.
Earlier, German defense company Helsing’s Ukraine-proven HX-2 drone performed successfully during tests with US soldiers in Lithuania.

articles.title: Russian Ballistic Missiles Hit Kyiv University Campus, Killing One and Injuring Nine
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russian Ballistic Missiles Hit Kyiv University Campus, Killing One and Injuring Nine
Editor’s note: this is a developing story.
UPD 2, 23:49 Kyiv time: The person killed was found in a partially collapsed three-story non-residential building in the Dniprovskyi district, according to the State Emergency Service. The injured were hurt at several locations in the Desnianskyi district, including the campus and dormitories.
UPD, 23:24 Kyiv time: One person has been killed and nine injured, most of them students living in a university dormitory, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
Russian ballistic missiles struck the territory of a local university campus, Kyoto Park, areas adjacent to a metro station, and nearby residential quarters in Kyiv on the evening of October 26, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
He highlighted that the attack directly targeted densely populated civilian locations with no military facilities nearby.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Zelenskyy stressed that artificial delays in supplying air defense systems to Ukraine directly assist Russian terror when cities face persistent strikes.
He called on international partners to fulfill defense agreements without delay and to provide Ukraine with the necessary capabilities to strike Russian ballistic missile launch systems as the most effective method to save lives.
According to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko, the Russian ballistic attack left one person dead and 9 others injured. Most of the victims were students residing in a university dormitory. Emergency medical services hospitalized nine of the wounded.
Among those caught in the attack was an emergency medical crew responding to a call near the Lisova metro station in the Desnianskyi district; a paramedic and an emergency medical technician suffered non-critical injuries.
The assault caused widespread destruction across the Desnianskyi and Dniprovskyi districts. In the Desnianskyi district, a missile landed near a university dormitory, shattering its windows and injuring a 20-year-old woman.
Blast waves also damaged a nearby residential building, where emergency crews suspect residents may be trapped under the rubble.
In the Dniprovskyi district, shockwaves blew out windows in the intensive care unit of one hospital and two departments of another facility, though no personnel or patients were injured. A separate strike hit a non-residential site near a local supermarket, killing one civilian.
On October 21, the United States restored critical early-warning intelligence sharing with Ukraine regarding Russian ballistic missile launches after a Russian strike hit a 24-story residential building in Kyiv's Sviatoshynskyi district.
The attack struck near the 20th floor, triggering a fire that killed two people and injured two others. Zelenskyy confirmed the resumption of intelligence cooperation following meetings with US officials, emphasizing that early warnings provided civilians with crucial time to seek shelter from incoming ballistic missiles.

What purports to be a reported Ukrainian drone attack on an ammunition depot in occupied Luhansk Oblast overnight on Oct. 27, 2026. (Exilenova Plus/Telegram)

Ukrainian forces attacked an ammunition depot in occupied Luhansk Oblast, setting off explosions at the site overnight on Oct. 27, monitoring channels reported.
Ukraine used strike drones in an attack that took several hours near the city of Khrustalnyi, according to Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova Plus.
Khrustalnyi has been occupied by Russian forces and their proxies since 2014 and is located about 65 kilometers (40 miles) southwest of the city of Luhansk.

A drone reportedly also struck a business center in Voronezh, as explosions and fires were reported across the city amid an ongoing drone attack, the outlet wrote.

articles.title: Two weeks after a Russian supply base burned in Luhansk’s Khrustalnyi, Ukrainian drones came back for an ammo depot
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones blew up a Russian ammunition depot near Khrustalnyi in occupied Luhansk Oblast overnight on 27 October, Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported. Drones also hit the oblast’s capital, Luhansk, for hours, and part of the city lost power. Russia’s occupation authorities have not commented.
Russia keeps pushing toward the last big Ukrainian-held cities in Donetsk Oblast. Its artillery there runs on shells kept in rear depots across occupied territory, and those depots sit within reach of Ukraine’s mid-range drones. Each depot lost behind the front pushes Russia to store and move its shells from farther back. That lengthens the supply runs Ukraine’s drones already hunt on the roads of occupied Ukraine.
Secondary detonations near Khrustalnyi lasted over an hour
The drone attack on occupied Luhansk Oblast went on for several hours, Exilenova+ said. Ukraine’s Defense Forces hit the depot near Khrustalnyi, and secondary detonations continued for more than an hour, the channel added. It posted night footage of a large fire glowing on the horizon.
Russia has occupied Khrustalnyi, formerly called Krasnyi Luch, since 2014. The city lies about 65 km southwest of Luhansk. It serves Russian troops as a rear and logistics hub.
Luhansk lost power as drones hit its former airfield
The attack on the city of Luhansk lasted more than four hours, Petro Andriushchenko, head of the Center for the Study of Occupation, said. Residents reported many explosions and fires in several districts, and the power went out. The main strike hit the city’s former airfield, he added. In October 2023, Ukraine’s ATACMS missiles destroyed Russian helicopters at air bases in occupied Luhansk and Berdiansk.
On Yandex Maps, the Russian online mapping service, the struck area near Luhansk airport is blurred, Andriushchenko noted. Yandex blurs military and critical infrastructure sites this way, he wrote.
Exilenova+ also reported a series of explosions in Luhansk. The oblast had been under a mass drone attack for an hour, with dozens of hits in different towns, Ukrainian Telegram channel DroneBomber wrote late on 26 October.
Neither side’s military has mentioned the attack on Luhansk Oblast. Ukraine’s General Staff left it out of its morning report. Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed it downed 222 drones over Russian regions, occupied Crimea, and the Black Sea, without listing Luhansk Oblast.
Pro-Russian local channels confirmed the attack from their side. A channel covering occupied Luhansk Oblast wrote that eyewitnesses saw a large fire and secondary detonations in Khrustalnyi. LIC, the news agency of Russia’s occupation administration in Luhansk Oblast, reported a series of powerful explosions over Luhansk and a visible glow.
The third drone night over occupied Luhansk Oblast in a week
Drones have now hit occupied Luhansk Oblast on three nights in seven days. On 21 October, they struck the seized telecom building in the city of Luhansk that houses the occupation’s mobile operator. Two nights later, strikes cut communications and power in part of the city.
Ukrainian drones just lit up Russian-occupied Crimea, Donetsk, and Luhansk — here’s how (video)
Khrustalnyi itself burned on 12 October, when strikes hit a former motor depot housing Russian troops. Ukraine also hit an ammunition depot there in June 2022. Back then, the site supplied Russia’s offensive on Sievierodonetsk and Lysychansk.
Blasts in Mariupol, Berdiansk, and Melitopol, and Russian claims from Bryansk
Occupied Mariupol heard two waves of explosions overnight, and the power went out after the attack, Andriushchenko also said. In occupied Berdiansk, several blasts near the Ekvator shopping center preceded a large fire, he added.
On the evening of 26 October, strike drones attacked occupied Melitopol in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Exilenova+ said. Locals also reported FPV drones hitting targets in the city.
In Russia’s city of Bryansk, Governor Yegor Kovalchuk claimed a night drone attack injured six people and damaged three apartment blocks. He said a man also died when a drone-dropped explosive went off. Yevhen Balytskyi, the Russian-installed head of occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast, claimed a drone hit a Simferopol–Moscow bus near Prymorsk, killing one passenger.
As the attacks began, Russian monitoring resources tracked up to 350 Ukrainian drones in the air, DroneBomber said. Most flew over Bryansk and Oryol oblasts, with more groups near Crimea, Novorossiysk, and occupied Luhansk Oblast.
Ukraine’s drones also weigh on Russia’s road to occupied Crimea. Truck traffic on the R-280 highway from Rostov Oblast has halved to about 1,000 a day because of drone attacks. Anatolii Tsurkin, who heads a carriers’ association set up in occupied Crimea, said so.
Kyiv set aside $113 million for the first phase of a program of middle-strike drones aimed at Russia’s rear. That makes nights like this one likely to keep coming for depots, airfields, and roads across occupied Ukraine.

articles.title: There were 16 ballistic missiles overnight — Zelenskyy on Russia's attack
articles.body:
There were 16 ballistic missiles overnight — Zelenskyy on Russia's attack
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy reported that Russia attacked Ukraine with 16 missiles and more than 280 drones. There are hits, and 12 people injured in the strike on a university campus in Kyiv.
Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles at Ukraine overnight on October 27. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported this while reacting to the enemy's overnight strike, UNN writes.
Consequences of Russia's strike on Kyiv
"The number of people injured after Russia's strike on the university campus and surrounding area yesterday evening has risen to 12, five of them students and university staff. While emergency services were helping people and dealing with the aftermath of the first strike, the Russians used ballistic missiles again," Zelenskyy said on social media.
What and where Russia attacked
A total of 16 ballistic missiles were launched this night. And more than 280 drones. Unfortunately, there are casualties and strikes in Kyiv, including on the Pivdennyi Bridge. This is a serious escalation in Russia's operation against our logistics. There were also strikes on Kyiv region, Vinnytsia region, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk region, Kharkiv region, Odesa region, Chernihiv region, Sumy region, Donetsk region, Kherson region and Chernivtsi region. Almost everywhere, Russia's targets are energy facilities, logistics and ordinary urban infrastructure
On Patriot and other air defense systems
"Artificial and prolonged delays in the supply of interceptor packages for Patriots and NASAMS, which have unfortunately occurred recently, are directly helping Russia achieve the goals of its terrorist campaign. Every such delay means another Russian strike hitting one facility or another. Unfortunately, strikes occur every day," the President said.
"Russia is constantly taking new escalatory steps. Pressure on Russia and real support for Ukraine are needed to change the situation. I thank everyone who truly supports our defense of life and understands the importance of support packages arriving on time. We must bring peace closer and save lives. articles.title: Ukraine Downs 2 Ballistic Missiles, 255 Russian Drones in Overnight Attack Targeting Kyiv
articles.body:
Ukrainian air defenses shot down or neutralized two Russian ballistic missiles and 255 drones during an overnight attack primarily targeting Kyiv, the Air Force reported on Tuesday, Oct. 27.
Russia launched the attack from 6 p.m. on Monday, Oct. 26, using Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles from Russia’s Bryansk region and 280 strike drones, including Shahed-type unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), Gerbera drones, and Parodiya decoys.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Of the Shahed-type drones, 69 were jet-powered, according to the report on Telegram.
As of 9 a.m. on Tuesday, Ukrainian forces had intercepted or suppressed 257 aerial targets: two ballistic missiles Iskander-M/S-400 type and 255 drones. These included 56 jet-powered Shahed-type UAVs.
Several strike drones remained in the air, and combat operations were ongoing at the time of the report.
Air Force said impacts from Russian aerial weapons were recorded at 25 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at 16 locations.
Separately, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) reported that Russian forces carried out more than 40 attacks across five districts of the Dnipropetrovsk region overnight, injuring three people in the Synelnykove district.
Fires broke out in a multi-story residential building, vehicles, private homes and outbuildings. Residential houses also caught fire in the Nikopol and Pavlohrad districts.
In the city of Dnipro and the Kamianske district, infrastructure was damaged and a fire broke out. Rescuers extinguished all the fires, the DSNS reported.
Molodist Film Festival Marks 55 Years, Bringing International Cinema to Kyiv Oct. 24-Nov. 1
Russian strikes on Kyiv overnight into Tuesday, prompted the closure of the South (Pivdennyi) Bridge, a major crossing connecting the capital’s eastern and western banks of the Dnipro River.
Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko released the first photos showing damage to the bridge as specialists assessed the extent of the damage.
The Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) also reported disruptions on the Green (Syretsko-Pecherska) metro line, with trains operating separately between Syrets and Vydubychi stations and between Osokorky and Chervonyi Khutir stations.
The bridge remains closed to traffic, and authorities have not announced when it will reopen or when normal metro service will resume. The crossing carries both road traffic and part of the Green Line.
In a separate development, Russian ballistic missile strikes damaged an administrative building in Kyiv’s Podilskyi district and non-residential buildings at two other locations.
The attack followed Monday evening strikes on a university campus and nearby residential areas that killed one person and injured over 10 others, most of them students.

It is also important for partners to understand that Ukraine needs the proper tools to destroy Russian ballistic missile launchers. articles.title: Germany’s Helsing Unveils Low-Cost Highspeed Drone Interceptors
articles.body:
Helsing, a German military AI company, unveiled its Contra AI-controlled autonomous air defense system via a video posted on X on Monday. Helsing described it as a cost-effective system optimized to tackle jet-powered drone and missile attacks.
Helsing’s Contra system is intended to solve the existing air defense conundrum where the only current way of effectively intercepting jet-powered drones such as Russia’s Geran 4s and 5s is the use of multimillion-dollar interceptors.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Contra is intended to control two relatively inexpensive interceptor missiles: the AD-1 Inferno and AD-2 Ambush said to cost less than $100,000 each compared with Patriot PAC-3 missiles at $4-5 million a unit and the NASAMS (AMRAAM / AIM-9X) at around $1million a throw.
The military issues website Defense News cites recent intelligence reports, that Russia is increasing jet-powered drone and cruise missile production, to as much as 4,000 units a month, which, along with launch sites, could bring parts of the EU within range.
Artificial intelligence and interceptor speed, the key
While still at the developmental stage, Helsing bills Contra, based on its well-proven Altra C2 platform, as an autonomous AI-based operation that will allow the real-time detection and engagement of hundreds or more drone and missile threats into a single air defense picture.
It is anticipated to be “field-ready” by late 2027, with Helsing saying its seekers rely on European supply chains and is free from Chinese components.
Russian Commander Complains NATO Testing Drones on Ukraine’s Front Line
Intercepts would be achieved through a combination of two, advanced radar guided, container-launched missile interceptors whose performance is designed to overlap and supplement each other’s capability.
The AD-1 “Inferno,” which Helsing Chief Executive Gundbert Scherf says is intended as the “workhorse” of the counter-drone system, is powered by a jet engine, and flies at around 700 kph (435 mph) at a range of around 20 kilometers (12 miles). It can loiter over a defended area, swarm with other interceptors, and make repeated passes.
The AD-2 “Ambush,” intended as a rapid interceptor against drones and missiles that break through the AD-1 “net,” has a solid rocket motor and is said to have a flight speed of Mach 2.5 (1,900 mph, 3,000 kph) at a range of in excess of 20 kilometers (12 miles).
Both systems are able to be redirected mid-course by the Contra ground stations with an onboard radar-seeker for all-weather terminal guidance. While designed for, and capable of, stand-alone operation, Helsing said the system is set up to rapidly integrate with third-party counter-drone systems including missile interceptors, lasers, and guns. The company said Contra has already demonstrated such hardware integrations to multiple military customers.
Niklas Köhler, Co-Founder and President of Helsing, says: “Contra ends the air defense dilemma: slow fair-weather drones, or million-euro missiles fired at cheap, mass-produced targets. Our AI links existing sensors and effectors in real time and adds our interceptors, AD-1 and AD-2. With jet and rocket propulsion, a low-cost all-weather radar seeker, and two independent European supply chains, they deliver autonomous fire superiority up to ten kilometers (6+ miles) high – affordable and at industrial scale.”

articles.title: How long will Turkey keep its troops in Syria and Iraq?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
How long will Turkey keep its troops in Syria and Iraq?
Turkish Defence Minister Yasar Guler has clarified that Turkey will retain its military presence in Iraq and Syria until certain conditions are met.
The original justifications for Turkey’s cross-border deployments have dwindled in recent years. Now, analysts believe Ankara is offering new justifications for its open-ended military presence in these neighbouring states.
“We are maintaining our military presence in Iraq and Syria,” Guler said in a recent interview.
“When we assess that the necessary conditions have been met in terms of regional and border security, the status of our base areas and our presence in the region will be reconsidered.”
Open-ended conditions
Turkey sent troops into Syria in 2016. Its cross-border operations primarily focused on targeting the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF).
The SDF were a coalition formed by the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK)’s main Syria affiliate, which became an invaluable ad hoc US ally against Islamic State (IS).
Early this year, following a Turkish-backed offensive by the new Syrian government of interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa, the SDF agreed to integrate its fighters into the new Syrian military.
Complete SDF integration could remove Turkey’s decade-long justification for retaining troops in much of northern Syria.
“Ankara conditions its decision to withdraw from Syria not only on border security and the elimination of the terrorist threat in Syria, but also on the al-Sharaa government’s ability to establish state authority throughout the country,” Suleyman Ozeren, a lecturer at the American University and senior fellow at the Orion Policy Institute, told The New Arab.
“This condition could signal Ankara’s desire to maintain a Turkish military presence and use it as leverage against, for example, Israel if tensions in southern Syria escalate into military confrontation between Syria and Israel.”
Consequently, Turkey’s military presence in Syria may continue even if there is a successful Kurdish peace process in Turkey.
“There may be mainly two minimal conditions: the total and actual disarmament of the PKK-linked groups in both Iraq and Syria, and the absence of Israeli military pressure on Syria,” Ozeren said.
In Iraq, Turkey has made repeated forays into northern Iraq’s Nineveh province and Iraqi Kurdistan as part of the conflict with the PKK. Turkey has had bases in these areas since the 1990s.
In the second half of the 2010s, it advanced deeper into the mountains of Iraqi Kurdistan, establishing and maintaining a vast network of outposts and forward-operating bases in strategic areas to relentlessly pressure the Kurdish fighters.
Now, with a major peace effort underway aimed at having the PKK lay down its arms for amnesties and a conclusive end to the conflict possibly on the horizon, Turkey’s justifications for these bases could become defunct.
Muaz Al-Abdullah, Middle East Research Manager at the conflict-tracking organisation Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), specified that Guler’s remarks aren’t a withdrawal signal.
Rather, he was merely articulating the “latest version of an open-ended condition” which Ankara adjusts as events change.
“In 2024, Turkey tied any exit from Syria to a new constitution, elections and full border security. Earlier this year it said the Damascus-SDF deal was still not enough,” Abdullah told The New Arab.
“Withdrawal is possible, because the presence is costly for Turkey economically and politically, but it will be slow and conditional.”
He also outlined how the minimum conditions for withdrawal differ by country.
“In Iraq, the PKK must be disarmed and out of Sinjar and Qandil,” Abdullah said.
“Since the (Turkey-Pakistan-Saudi Arabia) Mecca alliance, Ankara’s concerns now also include the weapons of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) and the threat they pose to Turkey’s ally Saudi Arabia, including PMF drone attacks on the Kingdom,” he added.
“In Syria, the minimum is a completed SDF integration, PKK cadres out of the northeast, and a Syrian army able to hold the border on its own.”
Reality on the ground
ACLED data has documented a rapid decrease in Turkish strikes in Iraqi Kurdistan in the past two years since the latest PKK peace talks began. In 2024, Turkey executed 4,861 strikes in the region. That fell rapidly to 634 in 2025, then to zero so far in 2026.
“The security case for staying is weakening, but the political conditions are not yet met,” Abdullah said.
In September, Turkey agreed to gradually withdraw from the Bashiqa base in Nineveh in tandem with Iraq’s removal of PKK-affiliated fighters from Nineveh’s Sinjar, the homeland of the Yazidi minority subjected to the 2014 IS genocide.
Abdullah described Turkey’s willingness to hand over Bashiqa as a “low-cost concession” rather than the start of any strategic withdrawal. Turkey only established its presence there a decade ago to train local forces battling IS. It is also the furthest base from Turkey’s border.
Nevertheless, it’s important since it is linked to a network of forward bases along the border that support Turkey’s broader counter-PKK mission.
“The handover is also a trade, not a gesture,” Abdullah said. “In return, Baghdad committed to establishing full state authority in Sinjar and removing PKK-linked groups."
The agreement also specifies a “gradual handover” tied to security steps taken on the Iraqi side. As a result, the withdrawal timeline is wide open to delay.
“The real test is on the ground,” Abdullah said. “An Iraqi commander expects Bashiqa to be vacated by the end of this year. If it is, that is a genuine signal. A phased withdrawal begins only when the forward bases start closing, not Bashiqa.”
Therefore, statements and agreements don’t reflect reality on the ground. What would be considered a clear signal that the Turkish withdrawal has begun, the ACLED expert added, is an “actual withdrawal on the ground rather than another statement of agreement between the two sides.”
Syria's status quo
Turkey’s support for Syrian government forces in their January offensive against the SDF proved vital. Ankara is still supporting Syrian government forces in their efforts to establish complete authority in hitherto SDF-controlled areas.
The situation remains unsettled, with ACLED’s Abdullah pointing to reports of armed groups, including the PKK-affiliated Revolutionary Youth Movement, opposed to the Damascus-SDF agreement still operating in those areas. Still, Turkey-Syria collaboration isn’t limited to the SDF.
“Basically, while the Turkish concerns are mainly related to the SDF/PKK activities in Syria, it is also related to the IS activities in Syria,” Abdullah said.
“So yes, the nature of the Syrian-Turkish relationship has changed mostly from cross-border operations and military support on the ground to more of intelligence and training collaboration.”
In his interview last week, Guler noted that Turkey has established “close coordination in the field of security” with Syria’s post-Assad authorities and seeks to “strengthen the capacity” of the new armed forces “to ensure the security of our borders.”
“While the al-Sharaa government has been pushing to take full control of the northern border and end Turkish military control there, Ankara has been pushing for at least a measured understanding with Damascus that would allow Turkish military presence to continue,” Ozeren said.
The Orion Policy Institute’s senior fellow contends that if the present Kurdish resolution process ultimately results in the PKK’s total disarmament and the return under amnesty of ex-PKK fighters to Turkey, then Ankara’s pretext for its military presence in Iraq will become unviable.
“However, two developments could alter the security landscape across the region: an expansion of the Saudi-led conflict with Iran-backed Houthis into a regional conflict, and an escalation of the US and Israel war against Iran into ground operations,” Ozeren told The New Arab.
“Such developments would force non-state actors, including PMFs in Iraq and PKK-linked groups in Iran and even Iraq, to reconsider current arrangements.”
That possibility could especially become a reality if Turkey decides to “pursue military involvement” through its commitments under the Mecca Defence Pact.
"If, and this is a big if, Damascus establishes full governance across the country, Turkey’s security- and defence-oriented influence may diminish, as the al-Sharaa government has tried to diversify its defence and military engagements with other actors,” he said.
In September, President al-Sharaa said that his country is “now entering the stage of giving legal status to the Turkish bases in northwestern Syria,” subject to the approval of the Syrian People’s Assembly.
He clarified that Syria does not have a long-term need for such foreign bases but also wants to “maintain diplomatic relations and mutual respect with neighbouring and friendly countries.”
ACLED’s Abdullah assesses that Sharaa’s statement implies that Syria doesn’t want any long-term Turkish presence on its soil to avoid turning the country into an arena of regional conflict.
That is especially urgent considering the growing tension between Turkey and Israel, which could transform Syria into a flashpoint between these two regional heavyweights.
Israel’s repeated targeting of Syrian airbases that Turkey evaluated for potential use demonstrated how quickly Turkey’s presence could potentially draw Syria into a regional confrontation.
“At the same time, Damascus cannot yet do without Turkish support,” Abdullah said. “As-Suweida remains unresolved, and IS and other groups may expand their activity.”
“Legal status for the bases is Damascus’s way of regulating Turkey’s presence now, so it can reduce that presence later."
In early August, Syria reached a memorandum of understanding on the future conditions of Russia’s access to the coastal naval and air bases of Tartus and Hmeimim under which the bases will become joint training centres after a three-month transitional process.
While Abdullah anticipates that’s the direction Damascus is pushing regarding the Turkish presence, he stressed that any comparison with Russia has significant limits.
“Russia’s presence is two bases far from Syria’s borders, and their value to Moscow is regional reach," he said. “Turkey’s presence sits on a 900-km land border and is tied to a security concern Ankara considers existential. That makes it much harder to reduce to a residual training mission.”
“Expect a smaller footprint over several years, but not a Turkey that fully leaves northern Syria.”
Paul Iddon is a freelance journalist based in Erbil, Iraqi Kurdistan, who writes about Middle East affairs.
Follow him on Twitter: @pauliddon
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Yemen’s Houthis say they hit Saudi Ras Tanura oil refinery with missile
articles.body:
DUBAI, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis said on Tuesday they had hit Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura oil refinery, the biggest in the kingdom, with a ballistic missile.
The group’s military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the strike had caused a fire at the complex, which also includes a shipping terminal, located on the Gulf, west of the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the strike.
Ras Tanura, which has a capacity of 550,000 barrels per day, was shut for a period in the early months of the Iran war as a precautionary measure.
The Houthi militia have escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia since September, opening another front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran.
Nearly all of Saudi Arabia’s oil exports flow through two main ports: Ras Tanura in the Gulf and Yanbu on the Red Sea, both of which the Houthis have attacked in the past.
Bloomberg News cited a person familiar with the matter as saying Saudi Arabia had contained a fire near Ras Tanura’s terminal in the early hours.
The Houthis have been regularly firing ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi airports, ports and oil installations in recent weeks. On Tuesday afternoon, civil defence authorities briefly issued an air raid alert in the Saudi capital Riyadh.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting against the Houthis in support of Yemen’s internationally recognised government said it had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Riyadh.
The fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce between the coalition and the Houthis, who control the Yemeni capital Sanaa.
On Monday, Mecca defence pact countries Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran to try to de-escalate the overall Middle East conflict.
Parliament in Egypt, which has said it is considering joining the Mecca pact, on Monday authorised the Egyptian military to help defend Saudi Arabia if asked.
(Reporting by Yasmine GhaniaWriting by Nayera AbdallahEditing by Michael Georgy and Peter Graff)

articles.title: Kyiv’s South Bridge Hit as Russian Ballistic Missiles and 280 Drones Hammer the Capital
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Kyiv’s South Bridge Hit as Russian Ballistic Missiles and 280 Drones Hammer the Capital
Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv’s South Bridge during a massive overnight assault that also sent 280 drones toward Ukraine, forcing the bridge to close and disrupting metro service across part of the capital.
Russia launched a massive overnight attack against Ukraine, sending 280 drones—including 69 jet-powered Shaheds—along with ballistic missiles, with Kyiv identified as the main target.
The strike damaged the capital’s South Bridge, forcing authorities to close it to traffic and suspend metro service across part of the city, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko on October 27.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Klitschko said specialists were inspecting the South Bridge to determine the extent of the damage following the Russian attack.
Traffic across the bridge has been completely suspended while the assessment is underway.
The strike also disrupted Kyiv’s Green Line metro service, with trains temporarily halted between Osokorky and Chervonyi Khutir stations. Authorities have not yet said when either the bridge or the affected section of the metro will reopen.
Klitschko also released the first photographs showing damage to the bridge following the attack.
Russia is increasingly targeting Kyiv’s seven bridges across the Dnipro River in an effort to divide the Ukrainian capital and disrupt transport connections across northern Ukraine.
Disrupting crossings over the Dnipro could effectively split the city in two, with consequences extending far beyond the capital.
According to Ukraine’s military, Russia launched Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles from Russia’s Bryansk region as well as 280 strike and decoy drones from multiple locations in Russia, the occupied Donetsk region, and occupied Crimea.
The drone force included Shaheds, Gerberas, Parodiya decoys, and other types. Sixty-nine of the Shaheds were jet-powered variants. Kyiv was the primary target of the attack.
Ukrainian fighter aircraft, surface-to-air missile units, electronic warfare teams, drone units, and mobile fire groups were all involved in repelling the strike.
By 9 am, Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 257 aerial targets, including two Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles and 255 drones.
Among the intercepted UAVs were 56 jet-powered Shaheds.
Several attack drones were still airborne when the preliminary figures were released, and air-defense operations remained underway.
Ukraine reported Russian strikes at 25 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at another 16 sites.
This is not the first Russian strike on one of Kyiv’s bridges. Previously, a Russian Shahed drone struck Kyiv’s South Bridge as a metro train crossed.
Passengers reported hearing an explosion and seeing a flash as the drone hit near the roadway. Smoke then appeared inside the carriage, ash entered through the ventilation system, and several windows were blown out.
