articles.title: Pezeshkian to Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi officials: Iran seeks cooperation, will defend rights
articles.body:
Pezeshkian to Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi officials: Iran seeks cooperation, will defend rights
TEHRAN – Senior officials from Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia — the three countries that recently signed the Mecca defense pact — traveled to Tehran on Monday for talks with Iranian leaders.
Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan's Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met with President Masoud Pezeshkian and with Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei.
Speaking at a joint meeting with the three visiting officials, President Pezeshkian welcomed dialogue among Islamic countries and stressed the failure of enemies to achieve their objectives against Iran.
"They imagined they could bring the Islamic Republic of Iran to collapse through pressure and aggression; but the result of these actions was the strengthening of internal unity and cohesion and increased solidarity of the Iranian nation," Pezeshkian said.
"Our people, despite the imposed losses and hardships, defended their land with power and steadfastness. The notion that the Iranian nation can be forced into surrender is a false and void notion," he added.
The president said the Islamic Republic of Iran pursues its legal rights within the principles and rules of international law, and relying on those very principles, will firmly defend the legitimate rights and interests of the Iranian nation.
Call for united front against Israel
Pezeshkian expressed hope that the presence of major and influential Islamic countries could play an effective role in strengthening regional stability and unity.
"We should not allow the Zionist regime to commit terror and aggression against any individual or country whenever it wishes. I am confident that if Islamic countries stand together and adopt a coordinated position, such actions cannot be repeated," he said.
"I believe that if we manage our differences and emphasize commonalities and shared interests instead of focusing on divisive issues, we can overcome regional problems more easily and effectively," he added.
He warned against interventionist and divisive policies, saying one of the objectives pursued in the policies of the US and the Zionist regime is to weaken regional countries, create rifts among Muslim nations and gradually weaken major Islamic states.
"We must, by strengthening mutual cooperation and supporting one another, prevent the realization of such objectives and not allow regional countries to be exposed separately to pressure and threats," Pezeshkian said.
He added that Islamic countries should move to meet each other's needs through constructive engagement, economic cooperation and the use of mutual capacities. "The notion that nations can be forced into surrender through pressure and sanctions is a void notion. The deeper and broader cooperation among regional countries becomes, the greater their ability to manage problems and confront external pressures will be."
Pezeshkian stressed that Iran, relying on domestic efforts, the support of the nation and the guidance of the Leader, will successfully pass through difficulties, adding that Islamic countries must understand the interconnectedness of their security and interests. Weakening any major regional country, he said, could pave the way for increased pressure and threats against other Islamic countries as well.
From words to joint action
Emphasizing the need for consistency between words and deeds in regional relations, Pezeshkian said: "We should not say what we do not believe in or fail to uphold in practice. We must, hand in hand, provide the ground for flourishing the region's scientific, economic, cultural, political and security capacities; develop communication routes, facilitate travel, turn borders into opportunities for cooperation and link the universities, scientific centers, traders and merchants of Islamic countries to one another."
He said expanding multilateral cooperation lays the ground for sustainable security, noting: "When science, culture, trade and economy cross borders and communications among nations expand, the ground for the spread of terrorism and insecurity will disappear. Therefore, strengthening scientific, cultural and economic bonds not only helps the development and welfare of nations, but is one of the most effective ways to consolidate collective security in the region."
Pezeshkian said any understanding reached in such meetings that leads to stronger regional unity, cohesion and cooperation will enjoy Iran's serious and all-out support, adding that focus must be placed on common ground and areas of cooperation and differences must not be allowed to hinder shared interests.
Nuclear rights and double standards
In another part of his remarks, Pezeshkian reaffirmed Iran's principled position on nuclear activities, saying the Islamic Republic is not seeking nuclear weapons and, as a member of the NPT, wants to continue its nuclear activities within the framework of international rights and obligations.
"Iran accordingly reserves the right to benefit from peaceful nuclear activities and expects these rights to be respected within the framework of international regulations," he said.
He criticized dual approaches toward Iran, saying: "Using the nuclear issue as a pretext for exerting pressure, threats, attacks on nuclear facilities, and claiming readiness for talks and dialogue simultaneously with attacking Iran is a contradictory and unconstructive approach that has undermined public trust and increased distrust among Iranian officials and people."
Pezeshkian said Islamic countries must, by strengthening their interactions and coordination, not allow such approaches to become a routine for dealing with regional nations. Safeguarding nations' rights, respecting countries' sovereignty, countering aggression and strengthening regional cooperation require common will and coordinated action, he added.
"The Islamic Republic of Iran is also ready, relying on religious commonalities, mutual interests and respect for nations' rights, to expand its cooperation with Islamic countries in this path," he said.
The officials of the three neighboring countries also held separate meetings with SNSC Secretary Mohsen Rezaei. At the end of the meetings, the four countries issued a joint press statement, stressing: "The participants agreed to continue talks to strengthen cooperation among the four regional countries, including in the field of peace and security in the region."

articles.title: War update: 196 combat engagements on frontline in past day as Russian pressure intensifies  on Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka axes
articles.body:
War update: 196 combat engagements on frontline in past day as Russian pressure intensifies on Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka axes
According to Ukrinform, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this in a Facebook update on the battlefield situation as of 8 a.m. on Tuesday, October 27.
Russian forces launched one missile strike and 72 airstrikes, dropping 247 guided glide bombs.
In addition, Russian troops used 9,679 kamikaze drones and carried out 2,518 attacks, including 12 using multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS).
Russian forces struck Bezsalivka, Korenyok, Tovstodubove, Ulanove, Rohizne, Neskuchne, Bachivsk, Vovkivka, Hirky, Novovasylivka, Mykolaivka, Yastrubshchyna, Marchyshyna Buda, Luzhky, Potapivka, Sopych, Kucheriivka, Stara Huta, and Kharkivka in the Sumy region, as well as Huta-Studenetska, Mykhalchyna-Sloboda, Karpovychi, Kliusy, Hirsk, and Yanzhulivka in the Chernihiv region. Korenyok was also hit by an airstrike.
Ukraine’s Missile Forces and Artillery struck three areas where Russian personnel and military equipment were concentrated.
On the North Slobozhanshchyna and Kursk axes, Russian forces conducted one assault, launched three strikes using five guided glide bombs, and carried out 44 attacks, two of them using MLRS.
On the South Slobozhanshchyna axis, Ukrainian forces repelled six Russian attacks. Russian forces also attacked on the Kupiansk axis, near Volokhivske, Okhrimivka, Shabelne, and Chuhunivka.
Russian forces launched three assaults toward Radkivka.
On the Lyman axis, Russian troops conducted seven assault operations toward Zelena Dolyna, Kolodiazi, and Lyman.
On the Sloviansk axis, Russian forces launched three attacks near Ozerne, Kryva Luka, and Mykolaivka.
On the Kramatorsk axis, Russian forces conducted no assault operations.
On the Kostiantynivka axis, 22 Russian attacks were reported. Russian troops conducted offensive operations near Kostiantynivka and toward Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka, Novoselivka, Raiske, Novopavlivka, Vilne, and Kucheriiv Yar.
Russian forces launched 26 attacks on the Pokrovsk axis, attempting to advance toward Novyi Donbas, Dobropillia, Vilne, Sviatohorivka, Svitle, Myrne, Serhiivka, Molodetske, Novomykolaivka, and Filiia.
On the Oleksandrivka axis, Russian forces launched one assault toward Piddubne.
On the Huliaipole axis, Russian forces launched 15 attacks, attempting to advance toward Ternuvate, Yehorivka, Rizdvianka, Vozdvyzhivka, Nove Zaporizhzhia, Verkhnia Tersa, Hirke, and Charivne.
On the Orikhiv and Dnipro River axes, Russian forces conducted no assault operations.
No signs of Russian forces forming offensive groupings were detected on the Volyn and Polissia axes.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Russia’s estimated total military personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, stood at approximately 1,581,840 as of October 27, 2026.

articles.title: One killed in Ukrainian strike on passenger bus – governor
articles.body:
One killed in Ukrainian strike on passenger bus – governor
A Ukrainian drone strike on a passenger bus bound for Moscow has killed one person and wounded several others, according to Evgeny Balitsky, the governor of Russia’s Zaporozhye Region, where the attack took place.
The attack was reported on Tuesday morning near the town of Primorsk, on the Sea of Azov between the towns of Melitopol and Berdyansk. The area, which Ukraine claims as its territory, lies within the zone of so-called “middle strikes,” where Ukrainian forces have regularly launched drone attacks on purported Russian military and logistics targets using the Starlink satellite system for guidence.
Balitsky said 31 people were aboard the bus, which was traveling from Simferopol, the capital of the Crimean Republic, to Moscow. He said the wounded were taken to hospital, while other survivors were provided with food and accommodation.
The incident comes amid a dispute between Kiev and Elon Musk over Ukraine’s use of his Starlink satellite communications network for military purposes.
Musk has accused Ukraine of abusing Starlink for deadly “middle strike” operations, saying the system was intended as a civilian communications service rather than an offensive military tool. He contrasted it with Starshield, SpaceX’s military-oriented satellite service developed for US government customers.
Media reports and statements by officials have offered conflicting accounts of whether Kiev has direct access to Starshield or relies primarily on civilian Starlink terminals. Kiev has accused Musk and US President Donald Trump of imposing speed restrictions on Starlink terminals that effectively prevented their use on fast-moving platforms involved in middle strikes. Russian media reported a sharp decline in such attacks this month.
While the Ukrainian military depends heavily on Starlink communications, it has other means of conducting strikes deep inside Russia, where Starlink does not normally operate. Long-range drones and missiles can follow pre-programmed routes and use AI-driven final stage guidance to strike Russian energy infrastructure and other stationary targets.
The Starlink dispute has unfolded amid wider tensions between Washington and Kiev over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities. The Trump administration has repeatedly asked Kiev to curb strikes on refineries amid concerns about rising fuel prices, while Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky has rejected claims that Ukraine’s campaign is contributing to the increase.
Global energy markets are under pressure from several factors, including the US war on Iran, the Ukraine conflict and depleted strategic reserves amid tight crude supplies.

articles.title: 7 big questions as Britain hikes defense spending
articles.body:
Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey arrives in Downing Street in London ahead of a roundtable with business leaders on Sept. 14, 2026. | Carl Court/Getty Images
LONDON — U.K. Chancellor John Healey is set to deliver an unexpected increase in defense spending at his first budget on Wednesday, as Britain strains to reach its NATO commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defense by 2035.
Healey — who quit as defense secretary in the dying days of Keir Starmer’s government over a funding row — hopes he can show how Britain will start to reach that target now that he's safely ensconced in the powerful Treasury.
Until last week, it was assumed that the top finance minister would defer decisions on ramping up funding until next year’s multi-year, government-wide spending review. So Wednesday’s move could represent an early win for the Ministry of Defence in Prime Minister Andy Burnham's new government.
Advertisement
But with regular warnings in the press and in public about Britain’s unpreparedness for conflict, there’s much more to watch for beyond Wednesday's headline hike. POLITICO walks through the seven key details and defense industry demands.
1) How will Healey play the numbers game?
Healey's government-rocking resignation back in June was explicitly over a refusal in Downing Street and the Treasury to commit to spending3% of GDP on defense by 2030.
Now that he is leading the Treasury, Healey is under pressure to deliver on that. But even that keeps Britain shy of the bigger NATO aim.
On existing plans, U.K. defense spending is set to rise to 2.7% next year and remain flat until 2030. Healey's first move will be to fill the £4.7 billion black hole in defense funding in the Defence Investment Plan — meant to overhaul the armed forces and improve readiness — published earlier this year.
More money is now expected beyond this, briefed to the media in recent days as a “down payment” towards spending 3% on defense by 2030.
But two government officials, granted anonymity like others in this article to discuss internal thinking, said the pathway to meeting NATO's larger, 3.5% target will only come in next year’s spending review, not the budget.
Advertisement
Even on the smaller measure, the margins for the chancellor are tight, with government spending rules and debt targets leaving little room for maneuver. Mike Martin, an MP on the House of Commons Defense Committee, told POLITICO: “They have got themselves into a straitjacket over defense spending and none of this will be resolved before the next election. This is why I think an early general election is inevitable.”
2) Will the chancellor move to funnel private capital into defense?
Britain's defense industry has long called for more direct government spending on domestic contracts. But the sector also wants more private capital flowing into U.K. firms, and will be looking to Healey to set the conditions.
The Financial Times reported last week that Healey will allocate £15.4 billion to the country’s National Wealth Fund and £5 billion to the British Business Bank — a share of which could end up with defense companies.
Two key details to watch here are whether the government claims this money counts towards its wider defense spending commitments, or whether any cash is allocated purely for defense firms. Potential reforms to and incentives for pools of private capital, such as pension funds and venture capital funds, to invest in defense would also be welcomed by the sector in this budget — but the industry may be left waiting.
One of the government officials cited above said that a Defence Finance and Investment Strategy is slated for December, with a Defense Investment Summit coming December 1.
3) Where does Healey stand on global defense team-ups?
On Sunday evening, the Treasury disclosed that it would not join the Canadian-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB) — a proposed multinational financial institution with its own AAA credit rating that aims to provide cheap loans for countries to invest in defense.
Advertisement
The U.K. had previously considered joining the bank, or merging it with its own separate initiative, the Multilateral Defence Mechanism (MDM) — a planned scheme for joint defense procurement, stockpiling and supply chains for member countries.
But a joint statement with Ottawa said that the institutions will now work in partnership.
The MDM currently has £400 million allocated from June’s Defence Investment Plan, while none of the other member nations — the Netherlands, Finland and Poland — have confirmed whether they have contributed capital to the project.
Now that uncertainty over Britain’s membership of the DSRB has gone, the government will be looking to flesh out its plans for its own MDM.
4) Can the chancellor slash energy and manufacturing costs?
Two industry figures told POLITICO that one of the biggest barriers to doing defense business in Britain — making it less attractive than other nations — is the country's comparatively high energy costs.
However, slashing costs for energy-intensive industries, including the industrial base of the defense sector is expensive, and schemes aimed at reducing costs — such as the British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme – already exist. Measures reportedly under consideration this time around appear to focus more on reducing households’ energy costs than on supporting businesses.
Advertisement
A third industry figure predicted that ministers would not offer immediate support for business energy bills because “every possible option” for instant help “is too expensive." But a defense industry investor said the Treasury is, however, looking at reducing the financial burden of machinery — which they said is a key issue for small firms wanting to ramp up production as part of the supply chain.
5) What does Buy British actually mean?
The government has been consulting with the defense sector and wider British industry over what exactly constitutes a British company under its plans to implement a new "Buy British" scheme.
The plan aims to bring together Andy Burnham’s pledges of re-industrialization and more evenly-spread growth across the country, and comes after the EU proposed its own Made in Europe procurement plan to try and boost the bloc's own firms.
The push is also designed to build sovereign capability, which has become increasingly important to Britain amid fears that the U.S. is an unreliable ally. The recent row over Ukraine’s constrained access to the Starlink satellite system has exacerbated such concerns.
Early suggestions indicate the government will take a broad definition — in a potential boost for multinational defense giants. Rupert Pearce, the Ministry of Defence’s National Armaments Director, told a recent industry event that, from his perspective, French defense company Thales, which has a headquarters in the U.K., “is a British company.”
6) Will Healey move further on AI and hybrid defenses?
Ahead of the budget, Healey's Treasury announced a series of AI-specific policies with potential defense applications.
Advertisement
These include £165 million for AI-driven detection and surveillance of biological threats — a move first teased by the boss of Britain's MI5 intelligence service.
The government will also put £60 million into its Sovereign AI fund to invest in British tech companies, including autonomous systems, robotics, and advanced manufacturing.
Watch to see whether the chancellor waves around more promises of boosting British resilience to malign actors on Wednesday.
7) Will Donald Trump even notice?
Britain’s comparatively slow progress on defense spending has already caught the eye of the Trump administration.
Warren Stephens, the U.S. ambassador to the U.K., warned earlier this year that Britain must make “sustained investment” in defense, rather than focusing on “other spending priorities,” and warned against “backloading” defense spending to a later date.
A lack of a meaningful movement on defense spending — or at least eye-catching claims from opposition parties that Healey has fumbled it — could grab the attention of Trump’s team this time around. The timing is tricky: the Pentagon is currently undertaking a review of American military assets stationed in mainland Europe and the U.K.

But with regular warnings in the press and in public about Britain’s unpreparedness for conflict, there’s much more to watch for beyond Wednesday's headline hike. POLITICO walks through the seven key details and defense industry demands.
1) How will Healey play the numbers game?
Healey's government-rocking resignation back in June was explicitly over a refusal in Downing Street and the Treasury to commit to spending3% of GDP on defense by 2030.
Now that he is leading the Treasury, Healey is under pressure to deliver on that. But even that keeps Britain shy of the bigger NATO aim.
On existing plans, U.K. defense spending is set to rise to 2.7% next year and remain flat until 2030. Healey's first move will be to fill the £4.7 billion black hole in defense funding in the Defence Investment Plan — meant to overhaul the armed forces and improve readiness — published earlier this year.
More money is now expected beyond this, briefed to the media in recent days as a “down payment” towards spending 3% on defense by 2030.
But two government officials, granted anonymity like others in this article to discuss internal thinking, said the pathway to meeting NATO's larger, 3.5% target will only come in next year’s spending review, not the budget.
Advertisement
Even on the smaller measure, the margins for the chancellor are tight, with government spending rules and debt targets leaving little room for maneuver. Mike Martin, an MP on the House of Commons Defense Committee, told POLITICO: “They have got themselves into a straitjacket over defense spending and none of this will be resolved before the next election. This is why I think an early general election is inevitable.”
2) Will the chancellor move to funnel private capital into defense?
Britain's defense industry has long called for more direct government spending on domestic contracts. But the sector also wants more private capital flowing into U.K. firms, and will be looking to Healey to set the conditions.
The Financial Times reported last week that Healey will allocate £15.4 billion to the country’s National Wealth Fund and £5 billion to the British Business Bank — a share of which could end up with defense companies.
Two key details to watch here are whether the government claims this money counts towards its wider defense spending commitments, or whether any cash is allocated purely for defense firms. Potential reforms to and incentives for pools of private capital, such as pension funds and venture capital funds, to invest in defense would also be welcomed by the sector in this budget — but the industry may be left waiting.
One of the government officials cited above said that a Defence Finance and Investment Strategy is slated for December, with a Defense Investment Summit coming December 1.
3) Where does Healey stand on global defense team-ups?
On Sunday evening, the Treasury disclosed that it would not join the Canadian-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB) — a proposed multinational financial institution with its own AAA credit rating that aims to provide cheap loans for countries to invest in defense.
Advertisement
The U.K. had previously considered joining the bank, or merging it with its own separate initiative, the Multilateral Defence Mechanism (MDM) — a planned scheme for joint defense procurement, stockpiling and supply chains for member countries.
But a joint statement with Ottawa said that the institutions will now work in partnership.
The MDM currently has £400 million allocated from June’s Defence Investment Plan, while none of the other member nations — the Netherlands, Finland and Poland — have confirmed whether they have contributed capital to the project.
Now that uncertainty over Britain’s membership of the DSRB has gone, the government will be looking to flesh out its plans for its own MDM.
4) Can the chancellor slash energy and manufacturing costs?
Two industry figures told POLITICO that one of the biggest barriers to doing defense business in Britain — making it less attractive than other nations — is the country's comparatively high energy costs.
However, slashing costs for energy-intensive industries, including the industrial base of the defense sector is expensive, and schemes aimed at reducing costs — such as the British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme – already exist. Measures reportedly under consideration this time around appear to focus more on reducing households’ energy costs than on supporting businesses.
Advertisement
A third industry figure predicted that ministers would not offer immediate support for business energy bills because “every possible option” for instant help “is too expensive." But a defense industry investor said the Treasury is, however, looking at reducing the financial burden of machinery — which they said is a key issue for small firms wanting to ramp up production as part of the supply chain.
5) What does Buy British actually mean?
The government has been consulting with the defense sector and wider British industry over what exactly constitutes a British company under its plans to implement a new "Buy British" scheme.
The plan aims to bring together Andy Burnham’s pledges of re-industrialization and more evenly-spread growth across the country, and comes after the EU proposed its own Made in Europe procurement plan to try and boost the bloc's own firms.
The push is also designed to build sovereign capability, which has become increasingly important to Britain amid fears that the U.S. is an unreliable ally. The recent row over Ukraine’s constrained access to the Starlink satellite system has exacerbated such concerns.
Early suggestions indicate the government will take a broad definition — in a potential boost for multinational defense giants. Rupert Pearce, the Ministry of Defence’s National Armaments Director, told a recent industry event that, from his perspective, French defense company Thales, which has a headquarters in the U.K., “is a British company.”
6) Will Healey move further on AI and hybrid defenses?
Ahead of the budget, Healey's Treasury announced a series of AI-specific policies with potential defense applications.
Advertisement
These include £165 million for AI-driven detection and surveillance of biological threats — a move first teased by the boss of Britain's MI5 intelligence service.
The government will also put £60 million into its Sovereign AI fund to invest in British tech companies, including autonomous systems, robotics, and advanced manufacturing.
Watch to see whether the chancellor waves around more promises of boosting British resilience to malign actors on Wednesday.
7) Will Donald Trump even notice?
Britain’s comparatively slow progress on defense spending has already caught the eye of the Trump administration.
Warren Stephens, the U.S. ambassador to the U.K., warned earlier this year that Britain must make “sustained investment” in defense, rather than focusing on “other spending priorities,” and warned against “backloading” defense spending to a later date.
A lack of a meaningful movement on defense spending — or at least eye-catching claims from opposition parties that Healey has fumbled it — could grab the attention of Trump’s team this time around. The timing is tricky: the Pentagon is currently undertaking a review of American military assets stationed in mainland Europe and the U.K.

articles.title: Russian attacks across Ukraine kill four, injure 55 over past day, as Kyiv comes under ballistic missile assault
articles.body:
Russian attacks across Ukraine kill four, injure 57 over past day, as Kyiv comes under ballistic missile assault
Russian attacks across Ukraine have killed at least four and wounded at least 55 others over the past day, Ukrainian authorities said on Oct. 27, as Russia launched an overnight missile and drone blitz against the capital, Kyiv.
Russian attacks hit Kyiv's Southern Bridge, disrupting metro services, as well as a university campus, an administrative building, and medical centers.
At least one person was killed, and 15 people were injured in the latest Russian attack on the capital, Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS) said. Those injured in the attack include a paramedic, a medical technician, and a 20-year-old university student.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russia attacked Kyiv with an unspecified number of S-400 and Iskander ballistic missiles, launched from Bryansk Oblast, and with 280 strike drones of various types, 69 of which were jet-powered.
Two ballistic missiles and 255 Russian strike drones, including 56 jet-powered drones, were shot down by Ukrainian air defense or suppressed by electronic warfare.
There were 25 locations reported struck by Russian munitions in the capital, as well as 16 locations that were struck by falling debris from downed missiles and drones.
In Chernihiv Oblast, six people, including a 12-year-old child, were injured in a number of Russian attacks, according to regional authorities.
In Chernivtsi Oblast, two men were lightly njured in a Russian drone strike, according to regional authorities.
In Donetsk Oblast, three people were killed and 22 people were injured in a number of Russian attacks, according to regional authorities.
In Kherson Oblast, four people were injured in a number of Russian attacks, according to local authorities. These included a 62-year-old nurse who was injured when a Russian "Molniya" drone struck a hospital in the city of Kherson.
In Sumy Oblast, three people were injured in Russian drone strikes, according to regional authorities.
In Zaporizhia Oblast, five people were injured as a result of Russian attacks, including a 17-year-old boy, according to regional authorities.

articles.title: Romanian intelligence uncovers Russian-coordinated sabotage network – suspects sought across several countries
articles.body:
Romania has uncovered a sabotage network coordinated by Russian intelligence services that attempted to set fire to the Carfil arms factory in Brașov on 14 September, the Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI) announced on Monday.
"Coordinators from the Russian Federation had assigned the group an extensive list of targets across the region, including state-owned and private arms manufacturers, as well as other facilities of military and industrial significance," Reuters quoted the SRI statement as saying.
The suspects include two Belarusian citizens and one Ukrainian citizen. Two were arrested in Germany while preparing similar acts of sabotage, while the third is being sought in Poland, according to Romanian television channel Știri.
Bucharest is seeking their extradition to Romania.
A year ago, Poland and Romania arrested eight people suspected of involvement in a Russian plot to send parcels containing explosives to Ukraine.
Romanian Foreign Minister Dan Neculăescu described the fire in Brașov as "part of a broader sabotage campaign across Europe" targeting the defence industry.
The SRI explained that individuals involved in such operations are typically recruited through social media, initially being offered money for "seemingly harmless tasks", such as "monitoring or photographing specific facilities".
"Later, the assignments become increasingly serious and may involve vandalism, arson or even murder," the intelligence service stated.
Russian President Vladimir Putin personally ordered an escalation of sabotage operations against NATO countries, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported on 20 October, citing three European officials familiar with US intelligence findings.
According to the newspaper, an unsuccessful drone attack on Germany's Leipzig Airport on 4 August was among the first operations carried out as part of the sabotage campaign.
WSJ sources revealed that following the incident, Russia warned the German government through an unofficial communication channel that Leipzig would not be the last target.
Russia reportedly decided to intensify its covert operations at a time when its armed forces were making little significant progress in Ukraine, while Ukrainian forces were increasingly carrying out strikes against targets deep inside Russian territory.
A series of further incidents followed across Europe after the Leipzig attack.
In August, drone manufacturing facilities in Estonia and Poland were set on fire.
During the same period, Slovak authorities announced that they had prevented an attack on a similar facility.
Poland, Lithuania and Bulgaria also reported acts of sabotage targeting stations associated with the Starlink satellite system.
According to Western officials, the sabotage operations are organised by the Special Tasks Department of the Main Directorate of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, established following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The unit is headed by Colonel General Andrey Averyanov.

articles.title: European countries with the largest defense budgets name Russia their main security threat and pledge continued support for Ukraine
articles.body:
European countries with the largest defense budgets name Russia their main security threat and pledge continued support for Ukraine
Defense ministers from the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, Poland, and France met in Paris on October 26 as members of the E5 group — the countries with the largest defense budgets — to discuss support for Ukraine ahead of winter.
After the meeting, the ministers named Russia the main long-term threat to European security and pledged to keep supporting Ukraine despite Washington’s warming relations with Moscow.
“Our countries share the assessment that Russia represents the most acute and long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security and stability,” the final statement reads. Russia’s war against Ukraine and intensifying hybrid attacks in Europe “do not undermine our unity, solidarity and cohesion. On the contrary, they strengthen our determination to pursue the efforts already undertaken to safeguard the integrity and security of Allied territory,” the ministers said.
The ministers pledged to continue backing Ukraine but announced no new military or financial aid packages, Bloomberg said. During the meeting, they limited themselves to reaffirming earlier commitments.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius stressed that the allies would work to preserve U.S. support for Ukraine: “We will do everything we can to ensure that the U.S. also supports Ukraine with supplies, as well as with intelligence and satellite data.”
The latest deterioration in relations between Ukraine and the United States is forcing Europe to consider how to help Ukraine without American support, Bloomberg said. Pistorius said the E5 countries are also working with Ukraine on their own air defense system meant to supplement the U.S. Patriot systems.
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have deteriorated sharply amid a fuel crisis. Donald Trump first demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian fuel infrastructure, and when a cease-fire could not be reached, he eased sanctions against Russia, allowing diesel fuel to be sold on the world market.
In response, Volodymyr Zelensky accused Trump of trying to force Ukraine into capitulation, saying the United States is delaying shipments of missiles for Patriot air defense systems and restricting the operation of Starlink and Starshield in Ukraine.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: US-brokered ceasefire begins in Russian-occupied Oleshky as strikes hit Kyiv
articles.body:
Announcing last Friday that she had brokered the ceasefire, Melania Trump said civilian officials from both Russia and Ukraine would visit residents in their homes and "determine the level of assistance they require".
A localised ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky went into effect early on Tuesday.
The local pause in fighting started at 3 am to allow an aid mission into Oleshky in southern Ukraine later this week.
According to her office, Melania Trump led talks with civilian negotiators from Russia and Ukraine after meeting with UN officials who briefed her on the situation in the town.
The aid mission is planned ahead of a new round of US-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine expected next month aimed at ending the war after more than 4½ years of fighting.
Up to 2,000 people are stranded in Oleshky with dwindling food and medicine. They are unable to leave because of explosive mines and drone attacks in the area, according to the UN.
Russian and Ukrainian negotiators as well as the militaries of the two countries confirmed in separate statements that the ceasefire had begun.
Announcing last Friday that she had brokered the ceasefire, Melania Trump said civilian officials from both Russia and Ukraine would visit residents in their homes and "determine the level of assistance they require".
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine," she said.
Newsmax, a right-wing US cable network, has said it had been granted "exclusive television access" to accompany observers entering the city on Thursday.
Kyiv struck by wave of Russian strikes
Minutes after 3 am, multiple ballistic missile explosions shook Kyiv and air alerts sounded in multiple parts of the country.
A Russian strike damaged a major bridge spanning the Dnipro River in Kyiv, the city's mayor said.
"A strike hit the Southern Bridge. Metro infrastructure on the bridge was also damaged," Mayor Vitaly Klitschko wrote on Telegram, with city officials adding that train services across the bridge had been suspended.
Late Monday, the capital also came under attack, when Russian ballistic missiles damaged the grounds of a university in Kyiv, killing one person and leaving 10 injured, city officials said.
Moscow's latest pummelling has damaged medical facilities in the capital, Klitschko said, adding that a "blast wave shattered the windows in (an) intensive care unit".
"At another medical facility in the same district, windows were also shattered in two wards. Neither patients nor medical staff were wounded," he said on social media.
In another attack, "a building in a non-residential area was also hit. According to preliminary reports, there is one fatality near one of the supermarkets in the area," Klitschko said.
A strike near a dormitory belonging to one of Kyiv's universities has shattered windows in the building, wounding a 20-year-old woman, Klitschko said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said "Russian ballistic missiles struck the grounds of a university in Kyiv and the area around it –- effectively the campus, Kyoto Park, the area near a metro station, and residential buildings."
"The missiles hit very crowded areas, and there is not a single military facility nearby. This was a strike directly on the city, on its infrastructure," he said on social media.
In Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, authorities said attacks late Monday killed two people and injured four.
“It is important that the world sees that Russia is showing nothing but a desire to kill and continue waging war,” Zelenskyy wrote in an online post shortly afterward.

articles.title: "Morally incapable" – influential Republican criticizes Trump for concessions to Putin
articles.body:
"Morally incapable" – influential Republican criticizes Trump for concessions to Putin
Kyiv • UNN
Mitch McConnell criticized Trump's policy toward Russia and the restriction of aid to Ukraine. He warned of Moscow's growing strength and threats to the United States.
Former U.S. Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell sharply criticized President Donald Trump over his policy toward Russia and attempts to reach an agreement with Vladimir Putin. In the senator's view, concessions to the Kremlin and restrictions on aid to Ukraine will not end the war but will only strengthen Moscow's position. He wrote this in a column for The Wall Street Journal, reports UNN.
Details
McConnell was outraged by Trump's words that Russia allegedly "is behaving quite normally toward Ukraine." The U.S. president made the statement in response to remarks about Moscow's violations of the announced energy truce.
The Republican called these words "factually incorrect, strategically naive, and morally untenable." He stressed that easing sanctions would only encourage Putin to commit further aggression.
McConnell warned of the danger of concessions to the Kremlin
The senator said that threats to halt military and intelligence assistance to Ukraine could allow Russia to achieve new gains on the front.
This will not weaken Ukraine's will to defend itself, but it could allow Putin to make progress on the battlefield that had previously been out of reach
McConnell separately criticized Trump's agreement with Putin on supplying hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel fuel to the United States. According to him, such a deal is unlikely to significantly lower prices at American gas stations.
The politician also stressed that a Russian victory would create far more serious threats to the U.S. economy and national security than temporarily high fuel prices.
McConnell recalled Russia's cyberattacks on U.S. institutions, its support for Iran, and Putin's cooperation with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. In his view, the strengthening of Russian influence in Europe would directly harm Washington's interests.

articles.title: Russian strikes on Kyiv kill one, damage medical facilities
articles.body:
Russian strikes on Kyiv kill one, damage medical facilities
KYIV – A Russian attack on the Ukrainian capital late on Oct 26 killed one person and wounded eight, mayor Vitali Klitschko said, adding that medical facilities and a dormitory were damaged.
Russia has intensified drone and missile attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks, putting Kyiv – a city of around three million people – on a near-constant state of alert.
Moscow’s latest pummelling has damaged medical facilities in the capital, Klitschko said, adding that a “blast wave shattered the windows in (an) intensive care unit”.
“At another medical facility in the same district, windows were also shattered in two wards. Neither patients nor medical staff were wounded,” he said on social media.
In another attack, “a building in a non-residential area was also hit. According to preliminary reports, there is one fatality near one of the supermarkets in the area”, Klitschko said.
A strike near a dormitory belonging to one of Kyiv’s universities has shattered windows in the building, wounding a 20-year-old woman, Klitschko said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said: “Russian ballistic missiles struck the grounds of a university in Kyiv and the area around it –- effectively the campus, Kyoto Park, the area near a metro station, and residential buildings.”
“The missiles hit very crowded areas, and there is not a single military facility nearby. This was a strike directly on the city, on its infrastructure,” he said on social media.
The strikes come hours before a truce in the ravaged Russian-occupied city of Oleshky was expected to start after months of reports that residents faced dire food, water and medicine shortages.
Moscow said on Oct 26 it would consider more local truces for humanitarian purposes but vowed not to let up in the overall pace of the war, even as the sides prepare to restart stalled talks under US mediation next month. AFP

articles.title: Air defenses neutralize two ballistic missiles, 255 drones in overnight Russian attack on Ukraine
articles.body:
Air defenses neutralize two ballistic missiles, 255 drones in overnight Russian attack on Ukraine
Ukraine’s Air Force reported this on Telegram, according to Ukrinform.
Starting at 6 p.m. on Monday, October 26, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with Iskander-M/S-400 missiles launched from Russia’s Bryansk region and 280 strike UAVs, including Shahed drones (69 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parody-type decoy drones. The drones were launched from Oryol, Millerovo, Kursk, Shatalovo, and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, as well as from temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in Crimea.
Kyiv was the main target of the attack.
The air attack was countered by Ukrainian Defense Forces aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare units, unmanned systems units, and mobile air defense groups.
According to preliminary data, as of 9 a.m. on Tuesday, October 27, air defenses had destroyed or suppressed 257 targets: two ballistic missiles and 255 drones.
Hits were recorded at 25 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at 16 locations.
Several attack drones remaine in the air, and air defense operations are ongoing.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Russian ballistic missile strikes carried out since the evening of October 26 affected six districts of Kyiv. A 46-year-old woman was killed, and 15 people were injured.
Source: Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine via Telegram

articles.title: Mecca pact countries in Iran in bid to stop war restarting
articles.body:
- Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iran in Tehran on Monday in an attempt to stop the Middle East war from resuming.
- Parliament authorised Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Monday to take "all necessary measures" to help Saudi Arabia to defend itself - a move that could push Cairo more directly into the conflict between the kingdom and Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis.
- The Jordanian military said it had struck "terrorist organisations" in neighbouring Syria on Monday in retaliation for a deadly jihadist attack on a church last week, hours after authorities arrested three men they accused of the killings.
- A ceasefire agreement in Gaza has not stopped what a group of independent experts commissioned by the UN say is genocide carried out by Israel in the territory, the team said in a new report on Monday.
Israel prepares to vote as Netanyahu faces a tight fight
Campaigning and ballot preparations mark the lead-up to Israel’s election Tuesday, widely seen as a referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu, the country’s longest-serving prime minister.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu boasted of his endorsement from Donald Trump on the eve of Israel's election, suggesting the two leaders could restart their war against Iran if he wins, after Trump said they should "finish the job".
"US President Donald Trump has come with a friendship that has never existed before between an Israeli prime minister and an American president. And it is doubtful we will ever have such a friendly president again," Netanyahu said in a televised appearance late on Sunday night.
"He has another two years, and he says he is calling on you to vote for me."
The British maritime security agency UKMTO reported on Monday that a vessel was on fire off the coast of Iraq, without specifying the cause of the incident or the status of the crew.
"UKMTO has received multiple third-party reports of a vessel on fire, 63 nautical miles southeast of Al-Faw, Iraq," it said.
"Crew status, damage assessment, and environmental impact are unknown at time of report," the agency added.
Al-Faw is a port town that sits on the Gulf, neighbouring Kuwait and Iran.
Syria closes main border crossing with Jordan after strikes
Syria closed the Nassib border crossing with Jordan on Tuesday, suspending passenger and commercial traffic in both directions due to developments on the ground in Daraa province, the Syrian General Authority for Border Crossings and Customs said in a statement.
The closure came after Jordan's air force struck what it described as militant hideouts in southern Syria, saying suspects behind last week's deadly church attack in the kingdom were linked to "terrorist groups" operating there.
The Nassib border crossing is Jordan's only passenger and commercial border crossing with Syria.
Syria says Jordan did not coordinate before strikes
Syria's government said Monday that Jordan did not coordinate with it before launching deadly strikes on the country's south in retaliation for a deadly jihadist attack on a church last week.
A Syrian government statement carried by state news agency SANA said "no prior coordination with the Syrian side was carried out concerning the military operation" by Jordan, adding that authorities were investigating the strikes and discussing them with Amman while stressing the need for joint security coordination in border areas.
Syria says death toll in Jordan strikes rises to 8
Syria said the death toll in Monday's strikes in its south had risen to eight, as Jordan said it had targeted "terrorist organisations" after a deadly jihadist attack on a church.
Health officials said "hospitals in Daraa province have received eight victims, including an elderly man and three children", in addition to four wounded, raising an earlier toll of five dead.
Jordan strikes militant groups in Syria after church attack
The Jordanian military said it had struck "terrorist organisations" in neighbouring Syria on Monday in retaliation for a deadly jihadist attack on a church last week, hours after authorities arrested three men they accused of the killings.
It said air force jets had "destroyed several terrorist positions" and killed and wounded "numerous members" of groups linked to the perpetrators of the church attack.
Syria's state news agency SANA, citing a local health official, said the strikes across Daraa province in the country's south had killed five civilians, including women and children.
Iran security chief says 'very good discussions' held
Iran's security chief said on Monday he held "very good discussions" with the three member nations of the Mecca defence pact, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, after their first meeting in Tehran.
"Very good discussions took place between us," Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told state television after the meeting with top officials from the three countries. "I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region... I sensed a very positive atmosphere in the discussions among the gentlemen."
The meeting, proposed by Pakistan, brought together senior officials from the three countries and Iran for talks in the Iranian capital.
Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry said earlier Monday that the meeting aimed to "de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis".
UN probe accuses Israel of 'extermination' in West Bank
Israel has committed the crime against humanity of "extermination" in the West Bank, while continuing to commit "genocide" against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, United Nations-mandated investigators said Monday.
The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry said Israeli forces had also committed other crimes against humanity and war crimes in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967.
The commission, which does not speak for the UN itself, first determined in a September 2025 report that Israel had committed "genocide" in the war on Gaza.
In a new report, which comes the day before Israel's general election, the investigation found that in the West Bank, through military operations reinforced by sustained settler violence, Israel has waged a "widespread and systematic attack" against civilians.
"The Israeli authorities and forces have committed the crimes against humanity of extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence in the West Bank, as well as persecution based on intersecting discriminatory grounds, with nationality, race and ethnicity at its core," it said.
Iran says agreed with Mecca pact countries on security
Iran said Monday it had agreed with three countries party to the Mecca pact, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan, that regional security should be ensured by countries in the region itself and not by foreign actors.
"The outcomes we agreed on were that security in the region where we live should be endogenous, meaning it should be achieved by the countries themselves, and that we must prevent any kind of foreign intervention in this region," Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei said after the meeting.
Israel dismisses UN-backed probe's report on genocide
Israel on Monday dismissed as "propaganda" a new report issued by UN-mandated investigators accusing it of committing the crime against humanity of extermination in the West Bank and genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.
The Israeli foreign ministry said on X that the investigators' finding "is not a human rights report but a propaganda document detached from reality, aimed at undermining Israel's right to self-defense, delegitimizing the Jewish state, and legitimizing jihadist terrorism against its citizens".
At least 1,500 Palestinians have been killed in the Gaza Strip since the so-called ceasefire took effect on 10 October 2025.
UN raises 'ethnic cleansing' concerns over Israeli operation
Israeli military operation in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron, launched after a deadly attack by Palestinian gunmen, raises serious concerns of "ethnic cleansing", the United Nations warned Monday.
Israel's "aggressive operation" has already resulted in the forcible displacement of thousands of Palestinians, "demolished homes and commercial property, and deprived residents of the ability to move freely", UN rights chief Volker Türk said in a statement.
"The sweeping steps taken raise grave concerns of unnecessary and disproportionate use of force, which must end."
He said the lockdown was confining many to their homes and immediate neighbourhoods.
Gaza truce has not stopped Israel from committing genocide
A ceasefire agreement in Gaza has not stopped what a group of independent experts commissioned by the UN say is genocide carried out by Israel in the territory, the team said in a new report on Monday. They also accused Israeli forces of crimes against humanity, including torture and rape, in the West Bank.
In response, Israel's mission in Geneva called for the commission's dissolution and said on X the report marked an example of the body's “misinformation campaign to demonise the state of Israel and portray its very existence as criminal."
Israel has long criticised the commission's output and denied accusations of genocide in Gaza and sexual assault by its forces.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has called for a just settlement of the Palestinian issue and comprehensive reform of the UN Security Council during talks with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.
Guterres welcomed Egypt's efforts to consolidate the Gaza ceasefire agreement, praising Cairo's role in facilitating the delivery of humanitarian aid and ensuring it reaches those in need.
"Lasting peace in the region could not be achieved without a just settlement of the Palestinian issue," Guterres said, stressing that it would remain the central issue in the Middle East until a final resolution is reached.
The UN chief also expressed deep concern over developments in the occupied West Bank and urged the international community to fulfil its responsibilities by taking action to halt violations against Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank.
Putin to meet Qatar's emir, Iran's president in Moscow
Russian President Vladimir Putin will meet Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Moscow on Tuesday, as diplomatic efforts intensify to end the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said the meetings would take place following a gathering of Gas Exporting Countries Forum leaders hosted by Putin in the Russian capital.

Putin will meet the two men after hosting leaders of a Gas Exporting Countries Forum in Moscow, the Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters.

More than 3,000 people have been displaced by an Israeli military operation launched in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron after a deadly attack by Palestinian gunmen, municipal authorities said Monday.

articles.title: Israel’s Mossad chief backed swift Iran operation opposed by army chief: Report
articles.body:
The head of Israeli spy agency the Mossad backed a swift military operation against Iran proposed by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while army Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir opposed it, Israeli media reported Monday, on the eve of the country’s pivotal general elections, with Netanyahu’s post at stake, Anadolu reports.
Daily Israel Hayom said Netanyahu pushed for the operation but faced opposition from Zamir, who had not been informed of it in advance, while Mossad chief Roman Gofman supported the proposal.
The daily quoted an unnamed source familiar with the discussions as saying the operation “could have led to renewed war with Iran,” although it would not have amounted to a resumption of an intensive military offensive.
Israeli opposition figures accused Netanyahu over the past week of seeking to attack Iran to influence the election results. However, an Israeli military official told the newspaper that the proposed operation did not involve restarting a large-scale offensive.
An attack of that scale would only take place with full coordination between Israel and the US and a decision by US President Donald Trump, rather than by Israel alone, the official said.
According to the newspaper, Israeli and foreign officials believe a large-scale attack on Iran is inevitable, citing what they called Tehran’s progress toward acquiring a nuclear bomb, with the remaining question being its timing.
The timing would depend primarily on operational and intelligence considerations aimed at preventing Iran from reaching a point of no return in developing a nuclear weapon, the report said.
Diplomatic sources told the daily that Trump wants to wait until after the US’ Nov. 3 midterm elections, believing an attack could be carried out just as effectively later.
They also cited concerns that an attack could drive oil prices higher and hurt the election results.
The newspaper also reported that Israel and the US are preparing a plan to bring down the Iranian government.
READ: Former Iranian President Ahmadinejad denies report alleging Mossad contacts
Reported row
On Sunday evening, Israel’s privately owned Channel 12 reported an “unprecedented” confrontation between Netanyahu and Zamir over political directives to carry out a military operation that could quickly lead to a confrontation with Iran.
The channel said the dispute had peaked over the preceding 24 hours, amid concerns within the military establishment that the Iranian issue could be used for political gains ahead of Tuesday’s Knesset elections.
Netanyahu has placed security issues at the center of his election campaign, while opinion polls suggest his bloc will struggle to secure the parliamentary majority needed to form a government.
On Sunday, he posted an AI-generated image depicting a nuclear explosion in Tel Aviv, accompanied by a warning about the danger of Iran acquiring a nuclear weapon and a call to complete the confrontation with Tehran during the two years left in Trump’s term.
Netanyahu has led a far-right government since late 2022, widely described as the most extreme in Israel’s history.
On June 13, 2025, Israel launched a large-scale attack on Iran targeting nuclear and military facilities. Tehran retaliated with missiles and drones before the confrontation ended with a ceasefire that June 24.
Then this Feb. 28, the US and Israel launched a war against Iran, which responded with attacks on Israel and what it described as US military facilities in Arab countries.
Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding on June 18 and began negotiations that later collapsed over disagreements concerning navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic passage for energy supplies and goods.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition intercepts 2 Houthi ballistic missiles targeting Riyadh
articles.body:
Şahin Demir
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said Tuesday that its air defenses intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthi group toward the Saudi capital Riyadh.
Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki announced the interception in a post on the US social media platform X, without providing further details on possible casualties or damage.
Earlier Tuesday, the coalition said it intercepted and destroyed three Houthi ballistic missiles targeting Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province.
It also announced the interception and destruction of four drones launched by the Houthis toward the kingdom’s southern region.
The interceptions came amid escalating hostilities between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition, which supports Yemen’s internationally recognized government.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition against the Houthis since March 2015, after the group seized the Yemeni capital Sanaa and other parts of the country in 2014.

articles.title: German troops test Auterion’s Talon drone interceptor
articles.body:
- Auterion showed its Talon interceptor drone on a test range with the Bundeswehr, launched from a rifle-style launcher and guided by a second soldier.
- The company says Talon can engage single drones and swarms but did not disclose its performance or any German purchase plans.
Auterion, the drone software company best known for the autonomy systems inside thousands of Ukrainian strike drones, has shown its Talon interceptor on a test range with Germany’s armed forces, the Bundeswehr, saying the system is built to take on both single drones and swarms.
Footage released by the company this week shows several German soldiers in Flecktarn camouflage working with the system on an open airfield, with one soldier firing the Talon interceptor drone into the air from a special rifle-style launcher fitted with an optical sight, while another soldier standing nearby guides the drone onto its target after launch.
Auterion did not say where or when the trials took place, which Bundeswehr unit was involved, or whether Talon destroyed any targets during the tests, and the company has given few technical details about the interceptor itself.
In the way it is used, Talon resembles Russia’s Yolka, a small interceptor drone that Russian troops fire from a handheld launcher at an aerial target that has already been spotted, and which uses an optical seeker and an onboard AI module to track its target out to about 3 km (1.9 miles) at speeds of up to 200 km/h (124 mph), although Yolka is described as a largely fire-and-forget weapon, while the Talon footage shows a second soldier steering the drone after launch.
Auterion’s chief executive, Lorenz Meier, described the company’s approach to interceptors in July, saying the first version would be simple enough for a soldier to point the interceptor at an identified target and launch it, with later versions moving into vehicle launchers, deeper integration with air defense networks and fixed installations to protect sites such as airports, stadiums and government buildings.
The company, which has a major hub in Munich, has been growing its business in Germany through a joint venture with Ukrainian drone maker Airlogix that was formed in February 2026 with backing from the German and Ukrainian governments, and the venture began serial production in September of more than 5,000 Seth X and Anubis strike drones under a German government-funded contract, using Auterion software for AI-guided terminal navigation and flight without satellite navigation.
Germany is buying several layers of counter-drone defense at once, and in November 2025 the Bundestag’s budget committee approved about €490 million (about $546 million) for MBDA’s DefendAir short-range anti-drone missile, while the Bundeswehr has also signed contracts for interceptor drones with other companies, such as TYTAN Technologies.

articles.title: Russia’s Strikes on Ukraine’s Energy Grid Amount to Crimes Against Humanity, UN Inquiry Finds
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Strikes on Ukraine’s Energy Grid Amount to Crimes Against Humanity, UN Inquiry Finds
A UN-mandated commission of inquiry has found that Russia’s systematic strikes on Ukraine’s energy grid amount to crimes against humanity, in addition to war crimes committed through deliberate attacks on civilian targets.
The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine, created by the UN Human Rights Council in 2022, set out its findings in a report published by the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR).
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The investigation assessed the impact of these strikes during the 2025–2026 winter, noting that hundreds of drones and missiles damaged Ukraine’s energy grid in increasingly frequent attacks starting in autumn 2022.
The report drew on testimony from 255 individuals across nine regions—Dnipropetrovsk, Kyiv, Kharkiv, Kherson, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Poltava, Zaporizhzhia, and Zhytomyr—as well as input from Ukrainian authorities, medical professionals, and non-governmental organizations.
The commission concluded that Russian commanders issuing the strike orders knew the targeted heating facilities in major population centers were essential for civilian survival, particularly during winter conditions.
Russian authorities had also publicly announced plans for upcoming strikes. Investigators established that the energy grid was targeted deliberately as part of a state policy intended to cut off electricity and essential services, deliberately causing civilian suffering.
While the panel also reviewed Ukrainian strikes against energy infrastructure in Russia and occupied territories, it was unable to analyze their effects further because Russia refused access and failed to respond to requests for information.
The commission emphasized that international law prohibits attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, demanding an immediate end to such strikes.
Regarding the recruitment of foreign citizens into the Russian military, the commission gathered evidence linking Russian authorities to human trafficking operations spanning 29 countries. Recruits were obtained through deception or coercion, with operations coordinated through international agents and agencies.
Intermediaries operating under the guise of legal, government-approved companies processed visas and travel documentation. Upon arrival, foreign nationals were forced to sign military contracts written in Russian before being deployed to frontline positions for hazardous assignments, resulting in numerous casualties, disappearances, and surrenders into Ukrainian captivity as prisoners of war.
Similar cases have also been reported in other countries. The Peruvian government, for example, has confirmed that 11 of its citizens who joined Russian forces have been killed, while 114 remain missing and three have been captured by Ukrainian forces.
According to Spanish news agency EFE, Peruvian authorities said that among Peruvians recruited into the Russian military were people who are now missing or being held captive by Ukraine.
Overall, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate has identified more than 28,000 foreign nationals serving in the Russian Armed Forces under military contracts, with the number continuing to rise.

articles.title: Ukraine Has Been Waiting Nearly a Month for Hegseth’s Signature on Missiles for the Patriot and NASAMS Systems
articles.body:
Ukraine has been waiting nearly a month for U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to sign off on delivering missiles for the Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated this.
He said Ukraine is working on several fronts: with the United States, European countries, and other partners with stockpiles of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles for the Patriot systems.
“In particular, we have been waiting for nearly a month for Mr. Hegseth’s signature on the missiles for the Patriot and NASAMS systems. I have instructed my team to discuss this once again with the American side. Discussions are also ongoing with other countries,” Zelensky said.
It was previously reported that contracts to supply missiles for the Patriot system are on Hegseth’s desk, but he has not yet signed them.
A high-ranking Ukrainian official described the batch of missiles—which, according to him, is awaiting Hegseth’s approval—as “significant.”
“It’s hard to call this a monthly delivery, since there’s no established standard for how many missiles are needed each month. However, it is a significant volume,” the official said.
Over the past 90 days, the U.S. has transferred only 24 anti-aircraft missiles for Patriot systems to Ukraine.
At the same time, Washington is delaying approval of missile deliveries that Ukraine has already paid for.
“In the early days of the war in the Middle East, countries used about 2,000 missiles in the first 48 hours. In the first 48 hours—2,000 missiles they received from partners. I, on the other hand, have received 24 missiles from our strategic partner over the past 90 days,” Zelensky stated earlier.
The NASAMS anti-aircraft missile system also uses American missiles, including the AIM-120 AMRAAM, the extended-range AMRAAM-ER, and the short-range AIM-9X Sidewinder Block II.
In Ukraine, the primary publicly confirmed missile for NASAMS is the AIM-120 AMRAAM, designed to intercept aircraft, cruise missiles, and other aerial targets.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Russia strikes Ukraine with 16 ballistic missiles – video
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: Russia strikes Ukraine with 16 ballistic missiles – video
Russia attacked Ukraine with 16 ballistic missiles on the night of 26-27 October.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter)
Quote: "In total, 16 ballistic missiles were launched overnight. More than 280 drones as well. Tragically, there have been casualties and hits in Kyiv, including on the Pivdennyi (South) Bridge. A serious escalation in Russia's operation against our logistics. There were also strikes on Kyiv, Vinnytsia, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kharkiv, Odesa, Chernihiv, Sumy, Donetsk, Kherson and Chernivtsi oblasts. Almost everywhere, Russia's targets were the energy sector, logistics and ordinary urban infrastructure."
Details: Zelenskyy said that 12 people were injured following a Russian strike on a university campus and the surrounding area on the evening of 26 October, five of whom are students and university staff. Whilst emergency services were assisting people and dealing with the aftermath of the first strike, the Russians deployed ballistic missiles again.
The president emphasised: "The artificial and prolonged delays in the delivery of interceptor packages for Patriot and NASAMS systems, which unfortunately have occurred recently, are directly helping Russia achieve the objectives of its terrorist campaign."
Background:
- On the night of 26-27 October, the Russians attacked Ukraine with Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles and 280 Shahed (69 jet-powered) and Gerbera attack drones and Parodiya decoy UAVs. The city of Kyiv was the main target of the attack.
- Early reports indicated that as of 09:00 of 27 October, Ukrainian air defence forces had destroyed or jammed 257 Russian aerial assets: two Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles and 255 Shahed (56 jet-powered), Gerbera and other types of drones.
- On 26 October, Zelenskyy announced that Kyiv had been waiting for nearly a month for Pete Hegseth to sign off on missiles for Patriot and NASAMS air defence systems, and instructed his team to discuss the matter with the US side again.
